4.3.	Coefficients of business residence’s spatial-temporal distributions
The business residence variable passes all the tests of the model and we conduct a cartographic analysis of the spatio-temporal distributions of the coefficients of the business residence vari- able at different time periods, as shown in Fig 5. With the exception of the southern part of the central city and some areas on the edge of the Third Ring, most areas have positive model esti- mates during the study period, indicating that the residential variable is significantly and posi- tively associated with residential DiDi trips, and consistent with previous related studies, residential factors have a significant impact on car-hailing trips [47, 48]. Among the morning peak 1, morning peak 2 and evening peak 1 models, the spatial distributions of business resi- dence variables show some similarity due to the obvious commuting characteristics. In the evening peak 2 model, the spatial distributions of business residence coefficients differs from that of the other models, due to the diverse travel demand of residents at night. The late night model captures the residents’ need for leisure time, leading to high absolute values in major commercial areas and in some residential neighborhoods.

5.	Discussion
It has been demonstrated that urban built environment factors such as density, diversity, and accessibility have significant effects on residents’ travel behavior [10, 12]. In this study, the
 

relationship between built environment characteristics and online car-hailing pick-up and drop-off in Chengdu, China, was investigated. The global OLS model, local GWR model and MGWR model each confirm that the selected data on drop-off and pick-up of DiDi trips are significantly correlated with built environment variables. The goodness of fit of the morning peak and evening peak models is significantly improved when compared with previous studies at the same scale [11, 24]. Overall, in this paper, the regression results of the MGWR model are better than those of the GWR and OLS models, allowing a better reflection of spatial heteroge- neity in the roles of different variables. Some key variables in the model are also explored.
Except for two models for late night, the correlation coefficients of the housing price vari- able in the remaining four models that pass the significance test are all positive, indicating that there is a positive correlation between housing price and DiDi trips. As a representative of resi- dents’ income level, to a certain extent, the housing price can reflect the consumption level of residents’ households. On the one hand, the higher the income level of residents, the more likely they are to take a taxi compared to other transportation modes. On the other hand, areas with higher housing price are located in the core business districts of Chengdu, such as Cao Tang Street, Chunxi Road, and Dongda Road, which are prone to serious traffic congestion caused by intensive traffic flow in the morning peak and evening peak, encouraging commut- ing by taxi instead of driving. This result supports similar findings in previous studies [11, 49]. In contrast, during the late night, it is difficult for the housing price variable to explain late- night car-hailing trips, due to the lower total counts of DiDi trips and the need for diverse lei- sure needs of residents and a small number of overtime commuters.
The coefficients of the business residence variable are higher during morning peak and evening peak than at late night, and residential trips are more likely to be influenced due to the needs of commuters. During the late night, DiDi trips are influenced by a combination of busi- ness residence, entertainment, and accommodation variables, perhaps reflecting the demand of residents for leisure and a small number of overtime commuters. In terms of spatial distri- butions, low coefficients are mainly located in the eastern and northern areas at the edge of the ring road. In comparison, the northern, northeastern, and eastern regions have lower housing price (Fig 3). According to the survey, this part of the region is mainly in Jinniu District and Chenghua District, and is dominated by warehousing, logistics and manufacturing plants.
Consequently, foreign laborers, wage earners and low-income families tend to live in this area. On the other hand, in the southern and southwestern regions, the population is lower but has a higher level of housing price, and its business residence coefficient fluctuates around zero.
This is mainly an affluent residential area in the traditional sense, where convenient private cars make residents more likely to travel by car, but higher income levels also allow them to accept the burden of traveling by taxi. Overall, they are likely to have a higher degree of flexibil- ity for DiDi trips.
The correlation coefficient for the internal traffic variable is negative in the evening peak model, which means that residents’ choice for DiDi trips when commuting from work is still strongly influenced by the subway and public transportation. Residents may be more willing to take the more cost-effective public transportation when in close proximity to subway and bus stations, all other things being equal. Meanwhile, residents located farther away from pub- lic transportation services will have less access to them, and are more likely to take a taxi for their off-duty commute. In addition, more planned public transportation trips by residents during the morning peak may cause the internal traffic variable to have a reduced effect on DiDi trips, such that the internal traffic does not pass the significance test during this period.
Among the other land use type variables, corporation is significantly positively correlated in the morning peak 2 model but insignificantly correlated in the evening peak model, proba- bly due to more diverse travel demand and destinations. Scenic spot is positively correlated in
 

the evening peak model, which indicates that the proximity to scenic spot is also one of the potential sources of DiDi trips. During the late night, in addition to the demand for entertain- ment, the accommodation demand also has a significant impact on DiDi trips. Unexpectedly, the road, HHI index and intercity transportation facilities variables do not pass the model sig- nificance test, which may be related to the small-scale research grid employed in this paper.


6.	Conclusion
This paper explored the association between online car-hailing and built environment charac- teristics in Chengdu, at the small grid scale, based on the MGWR model. The main findings are summarized as follows. First, we set up a 200m small-scale research grid, and analyse the spatial and temporal distributions characteristics of residents’ online car-hailing trips using DiDi order trajectory data, and extract the typical time periods as our research periods. Sec- ond, after a comparative study under this grid, the MGWR model fits better than the GWR and OLS models in this paper, and some of the models fit better than related studies by previ- ous scholars. Our study demonstrates the good applicability of the MGWR model when study- ing the relationship between DiDi trips and built environment in small-scale study area. The MGWR model shows that housing price, population, and internal traffic have a significant effect on residents’ trips in the peak hour model; business residence is positively associated with pick-up and drop-off in all models; and entertainment, scenic spot, and accommodation have a stronger effect on DiDi trips in evening peak and late night. Finally, the study finds sig- nificant spatial heterogeneity in the impact of built environment variables on car-hailing trips, of which we explore the spatial heterogeneity of variables for business residence that passes all model tests. The coefficients of the business residence variable are found to vary significantly across regions due to a number of factors including population, average housing price, popula- tion density and industrial structure layout. These findings can be used to inform the relevant authorities in some of the following ways:
First, during weekdays, there are distinct peak and low hours for residents’ car-hailing, with residents having higher demand for travel between 6:00–10:00, 12:00–14:00 and 16:00–19:00 than during other hours. When adjusting their operating strategies, transport authorities should focus on these peak hours and should adjust or reserve vehicle capacity to cope with them. At the same time, with limited vehicles and road infrastructure, they should encourage carpooling by residents during peak hours to reduce the pressure on car-hailing trips.
Second, in the spatial distributions of residents’ trips throughout the day, the volume and extent of trips during the late night are the smallest, mainly concentrated in the major com- mercial centres in the north, east and south areas of the Second Ring Road, near railway sta- tions and university campuses; during the morning and evening peak, the hot areas for trips are centred on major commercial areas such as Chunxi Road and Jianjian North Road within the Second Ring Road, and are sparsely distributed in a radial pattern along the main roads and residential areas towards the Third Ring Road. The maximum number of trips per day occurs during the evening peak. Online car-hailing companies should allocate appropriate vehicles to these hot areas of demand in advance to reduce unnecessary waiting for drivers and passengers. Residents should also try to stagger their trips during peak hours to avoid areas of peak demand for taxis, which is more conducive to convenient and efficient travel.
Third, the business residential variable has a significant impact on the amount of residential trips. Housing price, population and internal traffic have a significant impact on residential trips during peak hours, and residents have a greater demand for leisure and entertainment during the evening peak and late night. When cruising, online car-hailing drivers can precisely travel to areas with more of these variables to find passengers and tend to have a greater chance
 

of picking up passengers. Also, planning the location of future journeys in advance can help drivers effectively avoid traffic congestion and improve the efficiency of urban mobility.
Fourth, the built environment variables affecting residential trips are significantly spatially heterogeneous. During peak hours, the business residence variable has a significant negative effect on DiDi trips in the edge of the Third Ring Road and the southern part of the Second Ring Road, and a significant positive effect on DiDi trips in the northern, eastern, southeastern and northern edge of the Second Ring Road, indicating that the residential variable has a large spatial heterogeneity in its effect on residents’ trips, which is mainly caused by the combination of factors such as regional population density, income level and industrial layout. The lack of supporting facilities can easily lead to uneven distributions of traffic resources and greater pressure on traffic, and a reasonable variety of supporting facilities is more conducive to con- venient travel and efficient operation of urban traffic in the future.
Fifth, in general, residential demand for car-hailing trips is influenced to a large extent by variables in the built environment within a region and by the joint effects between neighbour- ing regions. Although a single variable in the built environment has an impact on residents’ trips by DiDi, it does not explain the entire travel process of residents. Therefore, in the process of urban planning by urban authorities, the division of urban functional areas should be taken into account and the internal structure of urban spatial units should be further optimised.


7.	Limitations and future work
There are still some limitations here that need to be addressed in the future.
First, in addition to the influence of the built environment, the age, gender and education quality of the residents also have a strong subjective effect on the online car-hailing trips. How- ever, due to data acquisition constraints, the corresponding population data are not available in Chengdu, more research on subjective factors of residents is needed in the future.
Second, this paper adopts a small-scale research grid of 200m x 200m. Consequently, there may be schools, hospitals and other large units that are divided, resulting in statistical errors. In addition, the trip destination is not always in the same neighborhood as the drop-off, and there is the possibility of travel to adjacent grid cells depending on the influence of the sur- rounding POI. How to measure this influence is still pending further research.
Third, in terms of the study period and region, the paper only selects data representative of DiDi trips within Chengdu’s third ring on weekdays. The dataset does not expand to other regions and time periods due to the more remote location of the airport and the atypical com- muting characteristics on weekends. Future studies with more data and in a larger study area should be considered to further validate our findings.

Faced with the increasing social and environmental challenges posed by overpopulation, traﬃc congestion, climate change, and en- ergy consumption, many governments worldwide have prioritized public transportation and focused on improving public transportation services (Vuchic, 2007). Recently, China began the Thirteenth Five- Year Program, which is intended to increase the public transport usage rate to more than 50%, thus alleviating traﬃc congestion and reducing transportation-related emissions in the cities (MOT China, 2017). However, public transportation continues to be used relatively infre- quently in many countries (APTA, 2016). For example, in the United States, only 5.3% of trips are made using general public transportation system (including buses, light rail, subways, metro systems, and taxis) in many cities (PTFT, 2016). Understanding urban public transporta- tion ridership is essential for promoting public transportation.
Numerical studies have quantiﬁed urban ridership. The most widely
 

used models are the aggregated four-step model (McNally, 2007) and the disaggregated activity-based model (Bowman and Ben-Akiva, 2001). Both of these models oﬀer a basis for quantifying urban rider- ship; however, they have weaknesses, including their high cost, low accuracy, and lack of elasticity (Gutiérrez et al., 2011; Zhao et  al., 2014). An alternative approach that integrates geographic information systems (GIS) and multivariate analysis has been developed to explore urban ridership. The direct association between the ridership of one mode public transportation (i.e., buses, metro systems, light rail, taxis) and potential demographic, land use, and transportation factors has been revealed (Taylor and Fink, 2003; Kuby et al., 2004; Chow et al., 2006; Yao, 2007; Zhang and Wang, 2014; Kepaptsoglou et al., 2017).  For example, Gutiérrez et al. (2011) developed a distance-decay weighted regression function to model the metro ridership in Madrid. Chakour and Eluru (2016) examined the association of bus ridership and stop-level infrastructure and the built environment in Montreal using a composite marginal likelihood-based ordered response probit

Focusing on subway operational factors, Ding et al. (2016) devised a machine learning method known as gradient boosting decision trees (GBDT) to estimate short-term station-level subway ri- dership. Empirical studies in many cities worldwide suggest that the signiﬁcant factors for urban  ridership  include  population  (Cardozo et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014), employment (Gutiérrez et al., 2011; Cardozo  et al.,  2012), land  use (Chakraborty  and Mishra,  2013; Hu et al., 2016), the presence of residential areas (Chiou et al., 2015), road density (Chiou et al., 2015), the distance to metro stations (Qian and Ukkusuri, 2015) and the presence of points-of-interest (Hu et al., 2016) Few studies have attempted to untangle the relationships between multi-modal public ridership and the potential controlling factors and compare them, thus providing a comprehensive understanding for de- cision makers to promote the sustainable development of urban public transportation. Furthermore, a case study of an Asian city is rare.
Exploring citywide public ridership confronts great challenges. In general, public transportation systems (including buses, light rail, metro systems, and taxis) are very complex. From a global view, buses, light rail, metro systems and taxis cooperate to fulﬁll daily travel de- mands and compete with one other (Cao et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017a; Zhang et al., 2018). Therefore, clarifying the inﬂuences on multi-modal public transport systems is a non-trivial task. Collecting multi-modal travel ridership data is an essential requirement. In addition, because public travels are driven by various human needs, and the level of urban functionality varies from place to place, the ridership distribution in urban areas depends strongly on the underlying urban form and functions (Pulugurtha and Aguila, 2012). Therefore, it is necessary to explicitly consider spatial variations when exploring urban ridership (Pulugurtha and Aguila, 2012; Qian and Ukkusuri, 2015). Geo- graphically weighted regression (GWR) analysis considers local eﬀects explicitly, thus oﬀering a reasonable explanation for spatial phenomena (Brunsdon et al., 1996) and a promising method to reveal the under- lying factors of citywide ridership.
Recently, information and communication technology (ICT) has provided us with massive amounts of useful transportation-related data, such as smart card data (SCD) (Zhong et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017b), bus GPS trajectories (Ehmke et al., 2012;  Tao  et  al.,  2014) and taxi GPS trajectories (Fang et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2018). Thus, we have an un- precedented opportunity to assess and characterize citywide human travel (Alsger et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2013) and ﬁxed activities (Yue       et al., 2014; Tu et al., 2017). Using SCD, bus and taxi GPS trajectories, and related GIS data, this article endeavors to reveal the spatial varia- tions of bus, metro, transit (the sum of buses and metro systems), and taxi ridership in a city and the driving forces. The spatially resolved eﬀects of a set of demographic, land use and transportation factors on the ridership of each form of transit are explored using GWR analysis.
 
The results of the model indicate that bus, metro, transit (equal to total bus and metro), and taxi systems exhibit common controlling factors, including employment, land use mix, and road density. The modes nonetheless exhibit non-negligible diﬀerences, such as bus accessibility, metro accessibility, and income. Such factors signiﬁcantly aﬀect taxi ridership, but not bus, metro or transit ridership. The spatial variations of the eﬀects are also visualized. These ﬁndings can help policy makers to attain a much higher public transportation usage.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. The next section in- troduces the study area and the dataset. Section 3 describes the meth- odology, including the dependent and independent variables, the global regression model, and the GWR model. Section 4 reports the results and compares them. Section 5 compares the results with those of worldwide cities. The ﬁnal section concludes the paper and suggests directions for future work.

2.	Study area and dataset

This study uses SCD, vehicle GPS trajectories, and related GIS data collected in Shenzhen, China, to investigate the spatial variations of multi-modal urban ridership. In this section, we outline the geography of Shenzhen, as well as the public transportation systems.

2.1.	Study area

Shenzhen is located in the Pearl River Delta, adjacent to Hong Kong. Since its establishment in 1979 as a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) of China, Shenzhen has become one of the largest and most innovative cities in China. Currently, Shenzhen has a residential population of over
10 million people and a mobile population of 6 million people (Shenzhen Statistics Department, 2015). It covers 1995 km2, 800 of which are built-up areas. As shown in Fig. 1, the city includes 6 ad- ministrative districts (Luohu, Futian, Nanshan, Yantian, Baoan, and Longgang) and 4 functional districts (Guangming, Longhua, Pingshan, and Dapeng). Luohu, Futian, Nanshan and Yantian belong to the old SEZ, which were well planned and built. Futian and Luohu are re- cognized as the city center, and they contain high buildings and are characterized by dense employment. Nanshan is the high technology district with many innovative companies and factories. Yantian is a port area for international trade. Baoan, Guangming, Longhua, Longgang, and Pingshan are suburbs that developed independently at the begin- ning of the SEZ; they possess compact neighborhoods with residential communities and factories, water bodies, mountains, and other features characteristic of open spaces. Dapeng is a tourist destination, and it contains mountains and beaches.
Since its founding in 1983, Shenzhen has experienced rapid growth in the ownership of privately owned vehicles and thus a dramatic in- crease in the use of privately owned vehicles for daily travel. However, for most urban residents, public transport remains the backbone of

According to the annual report of the Transport Commission of Shenzhen Municipality (TCSM), as of 2014, Shenzhen had 5 metro lines (Lines 1–5) that stopped at 118 stations in six districts, namely, Baoan, Nanshan, Futian, Luohu, Longhua, and Longgang. The bus system is composed of 874 bus routes and 47,798 bus stops, and citywide bus service is thus available to all residents. The taxi system consists of 16,152 taxicabs, which provide ﬂexible and swift travel service., Shenzhen is spatially partitioned into 491 traﬃc analysis zones (TAZs). Fig. 2 illustrates the spatial arrange- ment of the bus lines and stops, the metro lines and stations, and the TAZs. It can be seen that many bus and metro lines and stops are clustered in the southern part of Shenzhen, such as in Nanshan, Futian, and Luohu. Eastern Shenzhen, including Dapeng and Yantian, which are relatively isolated from the city center, are less serviced by public transport. Therefore, to avoid biases, we excluded Yantian, Dapeng and Yantian from consideration and explored only the bus, metro, and taxi ridership in the other seven districts.

2.2.	Dataset

The dataset in this study is mainly derived from two sources, spe- ciﬁcally, smart card data (SCD) for all cardholders and vehicle GPS trajectories that cover the period from September 24 to September 30, 2014. All of the data were provided by the transport operation com- mand center (TOCC) of Shenzhen, which is responsible for the
 
collection, storage, processing, and analysis of citywide transport data. The SCD were collected by the automatic fare system (AFC) on the buses and in the metro. The system contains all transactional records made by cardholders within the seven-day period examined in this study. Each SCD record indicates a tapping-in or tapping-out in a metro station or a bus. These actions are tagged with the time and either the metro station name or the bus identiﬁcation number. Notably, whereas the SCD in Singapore and Seoul recorded both the boarding and the alighting of a bus passenger, the SCD in Shenzhen recorded only the user id and boarding time. The alighting of a bus passenger is unknown. The vehicle GPS trajectories include bus trajectories and taxi trajec- tories. They were collected by the real-time traﬃc monitoring system, which records vehicle GPS locations at 40- to 60-second intervals. In total, there are 69.16 million SCD records (29.36 million bus SCD and
39.8 million metro SCD records) and 198 million vehicle GPS points. Additional GIS data, including bus routes and stops, metro lines and stops, and the transportation network were crawled from Baidu Maps, the largest map service provider in China.
Three ridership modes (metro, bus and taxi ridership) were ex- tracted from this massive SCD and GPS trajectory dataset. Fig. 3 illus- trates the data processing ﬂow. Metro SCD and bus SCD were ﬁrst ﬁl- tered. The bus GPS trajectories and taxi GPS trajectories were then separated. By fusing the bus SCD and GPS trajectories, the bus ridership was inferred. Metro ridership and taxi ridership were extracted from the metro SCD and taxi GPS trajectories, respectively.
A metro SCD records the metro station name and the entering/ leaving time. The transfer from one metro lines to another requires no additional swiping action. Therefore an individual's metro travel in- formation, including both boarding/alighting location and time, can be directly retrieved from the smart card database by inputting the long- itude and latitude of the metro station. In the case of metro ridership, 19.628 million metro travels (approximately 50.2% of total metro SCD) were identiﬁed based on the tap-in ﬂag.
The fusion of SCD and GPS trajectories to infer the boarding location in the case of buses is displayed in Fig. 4. Considering the bus routes and the road topology, the continuous bus GPS trajectory was recovered from GPS records by map matching (Xie et al., 2017). Then, each bus SCD record was linked to the corresponding trajectory based on the bus identiﬁcation number. The recorded time is used to interpolate the boarding location from the GPS trajectory. A delay at a road crossing was also modelled to obtain the correct boarding location. Following the direction of the bus route, we adjusted the boarding location to the nearest bus stop in the bus route. Using this method, the correct

Due to missing bus trajectories or positioning errors, 28.525 million (approximately 92.6% of total bus SCD) bus ridership were identiﬁed from bus SCD. The transfer between bus and metro or from bus to bus is not considered, as the alighting of a bus passenger was not recorded.
The taxi GPS trajectories record time, taxi location and service status. One ﬁeld named status (0 for idle, 1 for service) indicates whe- ther a taxi trip is being made. Accordingly, consecutive taxi GPS records for which the status changes from 0 to 1 suggests that a taxi trip has begun. Using this rule, we extracted all taxi trips, following the pro- cedure of Tu et al. (2016).

Spatial information such as population, employment, land use, transportation network, and bus routes were also collected. Using these data, we explored the spatial variations of urban public ridership and determined the factors that aﬀect them.

3.	Methodology

We utilized a global ordinary linear regression model and a GWR model to examine the factors aﬀecting bus, transit, and taxi ridership. This section describes the dependent variables, explanatory variables, and the models.

3.1.	Dependent variables

Using the massive individual multi-modal travel data described above, three types of urban ridership in each TAZ were calculated, corresponding to bus ridership, metro ridership, and taxi ridership. For the regression analysis, we also combined bus and metro ridership into the category of transit ridership.

3.2.	Independent variables

Many factors aﬀect urban ridership, including demographics and socio-economic, land use, and transportation factors. The independent variables used in this study were selected based on previous studies (Taylor and Fink, 2003; Chu, 2004; Chen et al., 2011; Gutiérrez et al., 2011; Osvaldo et al., 2012; Qian and Ukkusuri, 2015) and included demographics, land use and transportation factors.
The demographic information representing the characteristics of people is the main inﬂuencing factor of public ridership, as people make daily travels (Cardozo et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014; Gutiérrez et al., 2011; Cardozo et al., 2012; Qian and Ukkusuri, 2015). Population is  well recognized as a signiﬁcant factor aﬀecting transit ridership (Taylor and Fink, 2003; Ramos-Santiago and Brown, 2016). In fact, particular groups of individuals contribute substantially to urban ridership. Sample groups that make up a substantial portion of urban ridership include highly educated (Qian and Ukkusuri, 2015) and middle-aged people. Socio-economic factors, such as employment and income, are also factors that are generally recognized as being associated with ci- tywide travel (Taylor and Fink, 2003).
Land use is another important aspect associated with urban travel (Chakraborty and Mishra, 2013). In general, diﬀerent land use types

3.4.	Geographically weighted regression models

The GWR model explicitly considers the spatial eﬀects of in- dependent variables and incorporates the geographical coordinates of observations (Brunsdon et al., 1996). The GWR reveals the local char- acteristics of associated factors and is therefore very useful in in- vestigating spatial phenomena. The normal GWR formula is given by Eq. (5), where ri(u, v) denotes the dependent variable at location (u, v) and βik is the coeﬃcient of independent variable xik at location (u, v). In contrast to techniques that extract a unique coeﬃcient value for whole study areas, the estimated coeﬃcients vary from location to location, which represents the spatial aggregation of global statistics in the OLS regression. Therefore, the GWR model can characterize the eﬀects of the associated factors across the study area.

4.	Results and analysis

4.1.	Results of global models

The global models (OLS) were ﬁrst calibrated to determine which factors have signiﬁcant eﬀects on the studied urban ridership. The re- sults are presented in Table 4. The table reports the coeﬃcients and the t-statistics for each associated independent variable.
It is evident that no more than six independent variables are closely related to the ridership of the four forms of transportation. These variables are employment, income, land use mix, road density, bus accessibility, and metro accessibility. Judging by the adjusted R2, the selected independent variables can explain 65.8%, 67.19%,  80.56%,  and 82.83% of the variance in the bus, metro, transit, and taxi rider- ship, respectively. The smallest t-statistic value among the six in- dependent variables is 1.98, suggesting that all independent variables were signiﬁcant at the 0.05 conﬁdence level. Therefore, the four OLS models can provide a basic understanding of urban ridership.
The results indicate that several factors are associated with the ri- dership of all four forms of transportation, particularly employment, land use mix, and road density. Road density has a positive inﬂuence on bus, metro, transit, and taxi ridership. An increase in road density generates more urban travel by bus, metro (including the metro and the bus), or taxi. Improved bus accessibility can also encourage a greater number of people to travel, regardless of whether buses or taxis are used, but bus accessibility does not generate a signiﬁcant increase on the metro travel. Employment and land use mix are also positively as- sociated with metro, transit ridership and taxi ridership. This result suggests that increased job opportunities and diverse land use en- courage the use of metro and taxis. By contrast, these two variables are negatively associated with bus ridership. Counter-intuitively, fewer jobs may in fact increase bus travel. This result can be explained by the fact that most TAZs with high density jobs also have extensive metro sys- tems that attract greater numbers of people compared with buses. Fig. 6

One variable that is signiﬁcant in the taxi ridership model is not signiﬁcant in the models that characterize bus, metro, or transit rider- ship. Metro accessibility is not signiﬁcant for bus ridership, as the metro system only covers a few TAZs. Bus accessibility is not signiﬁcantly associated with metro ridership. Income is not signiﬁcant for metro and transit ridership because the metro charges low fares and oﬀers a good riding experience. People pay no more than 1 dollar and can travel    32 km by metro. The metro system also extends across the urban center and the city's satellite centers. People with diﬀerent incomes prefer the metro, as it provides a comfortable experience at a relatively low cost.

4.2.	Results of the geographically weighted regression models

The GWR models were calibrated to investigate the spatial eﬀects of
 
independent variables using the same independent variables used in the global models. Table 5 reports the estimated coeﬃcients and their de- scriptive statistics for the four GWR models. As discussed before, GWR models address spatially non-stationary problems, and the calibrated coeﬃcients of independent variables therefore vary in space. The ad- justed R2 values are 89.35% for bus ridership, 75.27% for metro ri- dership, 85.34% for transit ridership, and 89.97% for taxi ridership. Compared to the values given in Table 4, they correspond to im- provements of 23.55%, 8.08%, 4.78%, and 7.14% in the variance ex- plained for the bus, metro, transit, and taxi ridership, respectively. The reduction in the value of AICc also indicates the eﬀectiveness of the GWR models. Moreover, all of the Diﬀ values are less than −5.0, which indicates the degree of signiﬁcance of the independent variables. Hence, the GWR models can deepen the understanding of the spatial variation of four forms ridership.
The GWR results reveal that the actual eﬀects of the associated factors may be positive or negative and are highly sensitive to the un- derlying spatial background. Fig. 7 displays the spatial distribution of the coeﬃcients associated with employment. It can be seen that the coeﬃcients are negative in most of the TAZs for bus ridership. An in- crease in employment does not generally increase bus travel. This ne- gative eﬀect is partly due to the competition between the buses and the metro system implied in Fig. 6. Most workers prefer the low-cost and
 

 
Fig. 6. The density of bus routes and the geometry of metro lines.
 
comfortable metro travel if a metro station is nearby. Another possible reason is that north Shenzhen, which lacks a metro station, features many factories, with workers living in nearby neighborhoods. These workers make few motorized travels. Therefore, increased employment may not generate a signiﬁcant increase in bus ridership. However, the positive coeﬃcients corresponding to western and central Shenzhen suggest that increases in employment will increase bus travel in these places. Compared with the coeﬃcients associated with transit and taxi, the magnitude of this eﬀect is small, as the absolute value of the em- ployment's coeﬃcient for the bus ridership is less than 0.085, ap- proximately 17.8% of the max coeﬃcients for taxi ridership. With re- spect to the metro ridership, this result indicates the coeﬃcients are positive in most TAZs, except 15 TAZs in the Futian district, which is home to high income residents, who use the metro infrequently. Re- garding transit ridership, the eﬀects of employment are positive in all the studied TAZs (Fig. 7c). This result reﬂects the cooperation of the buses and the metro system to fulﬁll much of the demand for daily job- related travel, as the metro system covers the central parts of Shenzhen and its sub-centers, where most of the job opportunities are clustered. With respect to taxi ridership, the inﬂuences are positive in most TAZs, except in the Longgang center, as shown in Fig. 7d. This result occurs because Longgang contains many factories with a high proportion of employees living in surrounding rented rooms who thus make few trips. A similar pattern is observed in the coeﬃcients associated with land use mix. Fig. 8 shows the distribution of the inﬂuence of land use mix. The increase in land use mix generally induces a decrease in bus ri- dership, mainly due to the urban land use form. City centers, including Futian and Luohu, have low land use diversity but a greater number of bus travels. The remaining sub-centers and the suburbs have frag- mented and mixed-use land parcels as well as fewer bus travels. This spatial pattern can also be observed in the case of taxi ridership. The land use mix generates a decrease in taxi travel in western Shenzhen, an eﬀect that decreases with distance from the city center (Futian) or the sub-centers (e.g., Longgang). Mixed land use positively inﬂuences metro ridership in Longhua, Longgang and Luohu but negatively in- ﬂuences it in Baoan and parts of Futian. Mixed land use also positively aﬀects transit ridership, which includes metro ridership. Compared with buses and taxis, the spatial distributions of the corresponding coeﬃcients diﬀer, as these coeﬃcients are high in the north and low in the south. This result suggests that, taking the metro system into con- sideration, mixed land use will induce additional transit ridership,
especially in places without access to the metro system.
Road density also exerts both positive and negative eﬀects on bus ridership and metro ridership, as Fig. 9a and b show. Negative coeﬃ- cients associated with bus ridership appear in Shajin, the northwest part of Shenzhen. The factory workers there do not travel extensively, but the road network is dense. Hence, more roads will not naturally prompt an increase in bus travel in this area. In the case of metro ridership, the negative eﬀect occurs for west Baoan, near the Baoan Airport, and north Futian, near the Meilin Gate. Considering the sum of the bus and metro ridership, building roads will attract more people to use the public transit system, as Fig. 9c illustrates. The same conclusion can be drawn for taxi ridership, as shown in Fig. 9d. This conclusion is espe- cially true for Longgang in the northeastern part of Shenzhen, which has fewer roads.
Bus accessibility has positive eﬀects on bus ridership, meaning that an increase in bus stops and lines will encourage more people to travel by bus. However, diﬀerent patterns are obtained for transit and taxi ridership, as shown in Fig. 10b and Fig. 10c, respectively. The eﬀect of bus accessibility on transit and taxi ridership is negative in Futian and Luohu, where the buses compete with the metro system and the taxis. As people prefer to use the metro system, which oﬀers low cost and comfort, and the taxis, which are fast, an improvement in bus accessi- bility can attract more people back to using the buses. In other words, an increase in the supply of bus services will reduce travel by transit and taxi. However, the coeﬃcients of bus accessibility for transit and
 

 
Fig. 7. Spatial distribution of the coeﬃcients associated with employment.

 
taxi ridership are nevertheless positive in the northern part of Shenzhen, where public transportation service is eagerly desired.
The eﬀects of metro accessibility exhibit a similar pattern for metro and taxi ridership. An increase in metro accessibility will prompt more people to travel by metro. Undoubtedly, people prefer to use the metro system if there is a metro station nearby. This eﬀect is also positive in the case of transit ridership, as shown in Fig. 11b, and the same eﬀect was observed for taxi ridership (Fig. 11c). This phenomenon arises because TAZs with metro stations typically have high population den- sities and therefore attract more people to travel there, which in turn produces more taxi trips. The eﬀects of metro accessibility on both transit and taxi ridership display a minimum in the east and a maximum in the west, reﬂecting the underlying east-west spatial structure of the metro system. In fact, as Fig. 2 shows, four of the ﬁve metro lines (Lines 1, 3, 4, and 5) are oriented west-east. Only Line 2 in central Shenzhen runs south-north.
Income has a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on bus and taxi ridership only. Regarding buses, an increase in income encourages people to travel around. This association implies that people with higher income prefer to travel around to participate in activities. Regarding taxis, the asso- ciation between income and taxi ridership is negative in Baoan and Futian, as shown in Fig. 12b. This association arises in Baoan because very few taxi trips are made there, as Fig. 5d displays. However, in Futian, people prefer the metro system over taxis because of the con- gested traﬃc there. In addition, the increase in the coeﬃcient from the center (Futian) to the east (Longgang) suggests that increases in income give rise to increased taxi ridership.
In summary, the results indicate the spatial heterogeneity of asso- ciated factors' inﬂuence on public transportation ridership. The coeﬃ- cient of one factor (including the employment, land use entropy, road, bus accessibility, metro accessibility, and income) associated with dif- ferent types of ridership at one TAZ varies, suggesting the diﬀerent
 
eﬀects of these factors on bus, metro, transit and taxi ridership. The GWR further reveals that, from a global view, the spatial pattern of the eﬀects of a given factor on public ridership diﬀer, resulting in a complex spatial variation of public ridership.

5.	Discussion

To further understand the obtained results, we compared them with studies in worldwide cities, such as Montreal (Chakour and Eluru, 2016), Madrid (Cardozo et al., 2012), and New York (Qian and Ukkusuri, 2015). Tables 6 summarizes the results of these studies. The ﬁndings show that employment (or jobs) is signiﬁcantly associated with bus and metro ridership, echoing the cases of Montreal and Madrid in this study. Notable diﬀerences also exist, as Montreal and Madrid in- dicate that transportation factors, i.e., bus stops, metro stops, number of metro lines, and suburban bus lines, have considerable eﬀects on bus or metro ridership. The study suggests the mixed negative-positive eﬀect of employment and land use mix on bus and taxi ridership because of the spatial heterogeneity of the spatial, social and economic structure of Shenzhen, China, particularly the south-north diﬀerence in this rapidly developing city. Another reason is the cooperation and competition of multi-modal public transportation. The metro system completes a greater number of travels in the city center and fewer in the sub-centers and suburbs. Our study further reveals that bus accessibility and metro accessibility have positive eﬀects on bus and metro ridership, respec- tively. Considering the additional metro systems, metro accessibility also positive aﬀects transit ridership (which is the sum of bus and metro ridership). In the case of taxi ridership, income, road density, and metro/subway accessibility have a large inﬂuence on taxi ridership in Shenzhen and New York. More speciﬁcally, these factors have identical eﬀects in both Shenzhen and New York cases, with income, road den- sity, metro/subway accessibility having mixed, positive, and positive

eﬀects, respectively.
Our study suggests that diﬀerent modes of ridership in a city share certain associated factors. It also indicates that income, bus accessi- bility, and metro accessibility do not signiﬁcantly aﬀect transit, metro, or bus ridership. Furthermore, it reveals that one factor may have dif- ferent eﬀects on bus, transit, and taxi ridership and that these eﬀects vary across urban space. These ﬁndings provide insights that can be used to formulate eﬀective policies and projects to improve public transportation. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the spatial variation of urban public ridership that can help distribute available transport resources and thus encourage a greater number of people to use the public transportation system. For example, the results suggest that metro accessibility increases metro, transit and taxi rider- ship. Thus, improving metro accessibility by building additional metro lines may be a smart strategy for attracting metro riders. Doing so will have positive additional eﬀects on transit (i.e., bus and metro) and taxi ridership. Likewise, improving road density by building additional roads will make travel by transit and taxi more appealing, though this strategy may not be eﬀective in some places in the case of bus and metro travel because of the mixed eﬀect.
The results of this study indicate that the eﬀects of individual factors on ridership vary, depending on the form of transportation and spatial location. Therefore, a transportation policy should consider buses, the metro, taxis, and other travel modes such as privately owned vehicles and cycles. For example, the results suggest that greater bus accessi- bility has greater positive eﬀects on bus and taxi ridership in north Shenzhen. Thus, additional buses should be introduced to these places ﬁrst, rather than to south Shenzhen. Moreover, incorporating sig- niﬁcant independent variables with the characteristics of the under- lying urban area may produce more robust quantiﬁcations of multi- modal urban public ridership, thus helping regulate the supply of bus, light-rail, metro, and taxi services. As such, in attempting to promote
 
the usage of these public transportation systems, policy makers, land use planners and public transportation operators should work toward common goals in an integrated and collaborative manner.

6.	Conclusion

Understanding urban ridership beneﬁts the pursuit of a low-carbon comprehensive urban transportation system. However, limited eﬀorts have been made to investigate the spatial variations in urban public ridership and to distinguish the associated factors. This study presented a big data-driven comparative approach to examine the spatial varia- tions in typical urban ridership. Daily bus, metro, and taxi ridership were extracted from massive smart card datasets and vehicle (buses and taxis) GPS trajectories. OLS and GWR models were developed to iden- tify the associations between these forms of ridership and demographic, land use, and transportation factors. Taking Shenzhen, China as an example, an empirical study was conducted to examine the spatial variations in bus, transit (which was taken to be equal to the sum of bus and metro ridership), and taxi ridership and to compare the associated inﬂuences.
The ﬁndings of the study in Shenzhen suggest that bus, metro, transit, and taxi systems are signiﬁcantly aﬀected by three common factors. Employment, mixed land use, and road density, all contribute to improving bus, transit, and taxi ridership to diﬀerent degrees. Furthermore, the results of the GWR model reveal that the inﬂuence of these factors on the ridership of any particular form of transportation varies across the study area. Employment has both negative and posi- tive eﬀects on bus, metro, and taxi ridership. However, in the case of transit ridership, the eﬀect becomes entirely positive. Mixed land use is negatively associated with bus ridership, but becomes positive in cer- tain areas in the cases of metro, transit and taxi ridership. Road density is positively correlated with transit ridership and taxi ridership.

The results also indicate that the four modes ridership diverge in terms of income and metro accessibility. Income is signiﬁcantly asso- ciated with bus and taxi ridership. However, when the metro system is included, income is not a signiﬁcant determinant for transit, as people prefer the low-cost and comfortable metro and are not sensitive to the metro fare. Bus accessibility has a negative inﬂuence in the southern part of the city center but a positive inﬂuence in the northern suburban areas for bus, transit and taxi ridership. It is not signiﬁcantly associated with metro ridership. Metro accessibility has a signiﬁcant positive in- ﬂuence on metro, transit and taxi ridership, with an inﬂuence that in- creases from east to west. The association between metro accessibility and bus ridership is not signiﬁcant. These ﬁndings furnish insights for formulating policies to promote public transportation usage. They suggest that one operation (i.e., improving road density, increasing bus routes) may have complex eﬀects on diﬀerent public transport modes and therefore should be carefully distinguished.
In summary, the main contributions of this study concern the fol- lowing aspects. First, this study addresses a gap in the analysis of the ridership of urban public transportation by using massive vehicle GPS trajectories and SCD that cover the same period. A comprehensive understanding of urban public ridership including bus, metro and taxi ridership was reported. Second, the local variations of associated fac- tors were captured and visualized, helping to better understand the spatial heterogeneity of the determinants of ridership for diﬀerent forms of transportation. Finally, the comparison of the results for bus, metro, transit, and taxi ridership suggests that one factor may have quite diﬀerent inﬂuences on ridership depending on the form of transportation. This study therefore contributes to making more reli- able planning decisions and policies related to the urban public
 
transportation system.
This study has several limitations. It focused on the ridership of buses, the metro system, and taxis in Shenzhen. In future work, it will be meaningful to extend the study to include additional forms of transportation, such as cycles and privately owned vehicles. In this way, a total understanding of urban ridership can be achieved. The inter- action between bus, metro, and taxi ridership should also be in- vestigated. Finally, although this study is representative of China, we plan to conduct similar studies in other world cities, such as London and Singapore. The similarities and diﬀerences in the eﬀects of various in- dependent variables on diﬀerent urban areas will then be further ex- plored.

CHAPTER I AFRICA AND AMERICA

“That it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet saying, ‘Out of Egypt have I called My son.’”
 
The mystic spell of Africa is and ever was over all America. It has guided her hardest work, inspired her finest literature, and sung her sweetest songs. Her greatest destiny—unsensed and despised though it be,—is to give back to the first of continents the gifts which Africa of old gave to America’s fathers’ fathers.
 
Of all inspiration which America owes to Africa, however, the greatest by far is the score of heroic, men whom the sorrows of these dark children called to unselfish devotion and heroic self-realization: Benezet, Garrison and Harriet Stowe; Sumner, Douglass and Lincoln—these and others, but above all, John Brown.
 
John Brown was a stalwart, rough-hewn man, mightily yet tenderly carven. To his making went the stern justice of a Cromwellian “Ironside,” the freedom-loving fire of a Welsh Celt, and the thrift 16of a Dutch housewife. 	Literature review

	Relevant criminology theories

Various criminology theories have been developed to explain the occurrence of urban crime and provide prevention approaches, most of which consider place as a significant factor. For example, the routine activity theory suggests that the convergence of motivated offenders, suitable targets as well as the lack of capable guardian in specific space and time provides the conditions for crime commitment (Cohen and Felson, 1979). Furthermore, many theories emphasize the effect of environmental context. The broken windows theory points out that disorderly elements like broken windows, abandoned properties and litters indicate the lack of community control, and would eventually lead to more crime (Wilson and Kelling, 2017). The situation crime pre- vention (SCP) theory searches in the settings of crime occurrence for all kinds of proximate causes, such as access to facilities, natural surveil- lance, local laws and regulations, etc. (Shariati and Guerette, 2017). The theory of crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED) also asserts that crime incidents can be reduced by improving the quality of the built environment from several aspects such as access control, sur- veillance, target hardening, etc. (Cozens et al., 2005; Crowe and Zahm, 1994). In all, multiple theories have noted the effect of access to facil- ities, enlightening researchers to relate neighborhood function with local crime rate.
	Urban function data

As the completeness, granularity and availability of urban data gradually increased, thorough studies on the effects of urban functions on crime have become possible, in which land use data and POI data are two types of urban function data that are most commonly used.
Land use data, which represent land parcels as polygons and label them with urban function types, have long been used for modelling crime. Commonly, land use information can be derived from sources as satellite remote sensing and government authorities. While remote sensing images only reflect the natural properties of ground objects based on spectral characteristics (Yao et al., 2017), land use data from government authorities during planning activities emphasize the socio-economic functions of land parcels, and thus are more applicable for studying urban social phenomena such as crime. In this study, we focus on land use data of the latter category. The spatial units of urban land use data are generally street blocks or finer-grained parcels. As for time resolution, official land use data are often featured with relatively low update frequency, making it difficult for researchers to obtain up-to-date land use information that matches the time period of crime data, as in the cases of (Twinam, 2017) and (Wo, 2019).
POI data, which abstract physical facilities as points with socio- economic attributes, have emerged as an alternative to the conven- tional land use data for representing urban functions. Early crime studies obtained the geographic coordinates of commercial facilities from business data such as tax address data (Smith et al., 2000) and marketing website (Bernasco and Block, 2011), and it was not until the recent ten years that researchers started to collect massive POI data from map
service providers like Google’s Maps API (Bendler et al., 2014), Four-
Square (Wang et al., 2016; Zhao and Tang, 2017) and OpenStreetMap (Kadar et al., 2019) for better crime modelling. As a type of social sensing data, POI data are highly correlated with human activities. They record the locations, names and function types of places at the building level, and could be timely updated (Andrade et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022; Yue et al., 2017). Through machine learning, POI embeddings can further retain the latent semantic and spatial information of POIs and also make up for incomplete or inaccurate data (Yan et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2022). As the effectiveness of POI data in urban computing being recognized, they have gained increasing popularity in recent crime studies (Bendler et al., 2014; De Nadai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2016).

While POI data appear to have higher spatial and temporal resolution than land use data do, they do not necessarily lead to better explanations for the relationships between urban functions and crime. There are intrinsic differences between the two types of data in many aspects, such as their sources and forms, and they classify and represent urban func- tions in distinctive ways. Therefore, more thorough comparisons are needed before determining which type of data to use.
To attain a comprehensive knowledge of how previous researchers modelled crime with urban function indicators, related works are reviewed in terms of their focused functions, data, measures, main findings, etc. A summary of previous works by function categories is provided in Appendix A, Table A1.
	Urban function categories in relation to crime

Land use data and POI data resemble each other in the basic classi- fications of urban functions, among which residential and commercial functions are the most frequently studied ones. Other common function categories include business, education, transportation, recreation, pub- lic administration, etc. Nevertheless, POI data generally have much richer semantic features (Andrade et al., 2020), enabling further dif- ferentiation of urban functions. For example, FourSquare classifies POIs into ten parent categories and over 1000 subcategories (Foursquare, 2009). Using either land use data or POI data, researchers sometimes came up with divergent results when relating urban functions with crime. Main findings and controversies with regards to several common urban function categories are discussed as follows.
	Residential
Residential areas are perceived to be safer than non-residential ones, owing to informal social control from residents (Cozens et al., 2019). The majority of empirical studies also proved that residential land uses generally have negative relationships with various types of crime (Adel et al., 2016; Boessen and Hipp, 2018; Kinney et al., 2008; Sohn, 2016b; Su et al., 2023; Wo et al., 2024). Nevertheless, high-density residential areas are found to suffer from more crime (Kinney et al., 2008; Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009; Ando, Higuchi and Mimura, 2018). With POI
data, however, the effects of residence are sometimes overlooked. (Kim and  Lee, 2023)  didn’t found  notable relationships between residential
POIs and several crime types, and (Zeng et al., 2021) also found no effect of multi-story residences on theft crime, indicating that geographic points might be unsuitable for representing residential areas.
	Commercial
Whatever data were used, researchers generally concluded that commercial functions could significantly increase urban crime (Adel et al., 2016; Boessen and Hipp, 2018; Bowers, 2014; Kinney et al., 2008; Lockwood, 2007; Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009; Wilcox et al., 2004; Wo et al., 2024). However, the effects could vary across different commer- cial facilities (Sohn, 2016a). While land use data often treat all kinds of commercial uses as the same, POI data have more detailed classifications of commercial facilities, among which shops and restaurants are found to promote both property crime and violence (Bendler et al., 2014; De Nadai et al., 2020; Kim and Lee, 2023; O and Lee, 2016; Smith et al., 2000; Twinam, 2017; Vomfell et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021), alcohol-related places (bars, clubs and liquid stores) tend to attract vi- olent crimes rather than property ones (Bernasco and Block, 2011; He and Li, 2022; Smith et al., 2000; Vomfell et al., 2018), and hotels are less important (Zhang et al., 2022; Kim and Lee, 2023). In all, POI data could provide finer-grained pictures of the effects of various commercial fa- cilities on crime.
	Financial
Financial uses include business offices, banks and ATMs, etc. As for business function, office POIs are found to suppress theft crime and promote violent crime (Bendler et al., 2014; Kim and Lee, 2023; Smith

et al., 2000), yet previous studies failed to draw consistent conclusions with office land uses. While (Boessen and Hipp, 2018) suggested that office land uses result in higher level of several types of violence and property crime, (Wo et al., 2024) found positive effect of them on property crime and no effect on violence, and (Sohn, 2016a) suggested office land uses could decrease residential burglary. As for banks and ATMs, they are small-scale facilities and are generally represented with POI data, and most researchers found positive relationship of them with crime (Su et al., 2023; Yue et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2021).
	Education
The relationship between education functions and crime have been controversial. Theoretically, schools can either gather potential victims and attract motivated offenders, or produce positive socialization and guardians to improve neighborhood safety (Steinberg et al., 2019). In empirical studies, with POI data, most researchers believe that schools lead to more violent crime, while having no effect or negative effect on theft crime (Barnum et al., 2017; He et al., 2020; Vomfell et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022). With land use data, however, only some studies consider schools to be important factors triggering specific crime types like assault, property damage and motor vehicle theft (LaGRANGE, 1999; Wilcox et al., 2004; Kinney et al., 2008), while others found little effect of them on most crime types (Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009; Wo, 2019; He and Li, 2022).
	Transportation
For transportation function, most crime researchers focus on bus stops or subway stations using POI data, and claim them to be generators of various types of crime, especially property ones (Ando et al., 2018; Barnum et al., 2017; Bendler et al., 2014; He and Li, 2022; Kim and Lee, 2023; O and Lee, 2016; Yue et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). These transit stations are too small to be depicted with land use polygons. While transportation land uses can represent larger-scale transportation facilities like railway stations and airports, their effects on crime are seldom discussed.
	Recreation
Recreation functions can be undertaken by various forms of urban facilities including parks, playing fields, cultural facilities, etc. With land use data, recreation uses overall are found to increase crime rate (Wilcox et al., 2004; Lockwood, 2007; Kinney et al., 2008; Bowers, 2014), while parks seem to be insignificant (Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009; Sohn, 2016b; He and Li, 2022). By contrast, using POI data, parks, cultural and other entertainment facilities are all considered to be positively related with crime (Barnum et al., 2017; Bendler et al., 2014; He et al., 2020; Valente et al., 2024; Vomfell et al., 2018).
	Summary of inconsistencies
In summary, using either land use data or POI data, inconsistent findings have been drawn regarding the relationships of several urban functions with crime. For residential function, land use data seem to be more effective than POI ones. For education and office functions, more consistent findings can be derived from POI data rather than land use ones. For functions like commercial and recreation, the effects of the general categories are rather consistent using both data types, while POI data support further classifications and reveal that the subcategories indeed affect crime differently. Besides, some small-scale facilities like bus stations, banks and ATM can only be represented with POI data.
	Urban function measures in relation to crime

Beyond the classifications of urban functions, the measures of these functions also matter. To study routine activities and traffic patterns, (Cervero and Kockelman, 1997) have conceptualized the built envi- ronment into three principal dimensions, i.e., density, diversity and design (the 3Ds), with urban functions being an important part to be



Fig. 1. The 3Ds of urban function.

deconstructed. Fig. 1 illustrates the 3Ds with regard to urban functions. In criminology, the 3Ds are also thought to be able to change the mix of targets, offenders and guardians, and thus have great effect on criminal behaviors (Kim and Hipp, 2021).
Common measures of urban functions in empirical crime studies are consistent with the 3Ds as well, each of which has distinctive effect on crime. In this regard, density refers to how compact urban functions are. Compact neighborhoods are thought to either increase crime risk by
gathering more offenders and potential targets, or provide more natural surveillance through “eyes on the streets” (Jacobs, 1961; Kim and Hipp, 2021; Su et al., 2023). Since POI data present facilities as countable
points and could well support the measure of density, many studies calculate POI densities (or counts within an area) for various urban functions and relate them with crime. Most research find positive re- lationships between non-residential function density and crime rate, while the strength of effects vary across facility types (Bernasco and Block, 2011; O and Lee, 2016; De Nadai et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022).
Diversity refers to how mixed urban functions are. Similar to the case of density, there are debates on whether diversity has positive or negative impacts on crime. On the one hand, mixed functions bring about different times of use and ensure the presence of people, which could discourage potential offenders (Jacobs, 1961; Newman, 1972). On the other hand, the functional mix could be a cause of anonymity on the
streets, reducing people’s sense of responsibility and leading to higher
crime risk (Taylor et al., 1995). Several research have calculated land use mix with Herfindahl index or Shannon diversity index and examined their effect on crime, with divergent conclusions been drawn. Both (Jones and Pridemore, 2019) and (He and Li, 2022) believed that higher mix degree leads to more crime, while (Su et al., 2023) found the opposite. Other studies suggested that the impacts of land use mix vary across crime types as well as cities (Wo, 2019; De Nadai et al., 2020). Although the direct of effect remains controversial, previous studies generally agree that there are some relationships between functional mix and crime. As POI data gain popularity in recent years, researchers have just started to construct POI mix indicators for crime modelling (Kim and Lee, 2023), whose effectiveness needs to be further explored. Design refers to how urban functions are arranged, emphasizing the
provision as well as accessibility of amenities. By shaping pedestrians’
routines to their destinations, the design factors might bring offenders and targets together in specific space and time, facilitating crime commitment (Cohen and Felson, 1979; Cervero and Kockelman, 1997). Early studies constructed dummy variables to represent the existences of

specific urban functions, and found that the presence of facilities like malls, schools and playgrounds could lead to more crime (LaGRANGE, 1999; Wilcox et al., 2004). Later, fractions of urban functions became a more common measure to quantitatively depict the function composi- tions, enabling more accurate analysis on the effects of function pro- visions (Adel et al., 2016; Boessen and Hipp, 2018; Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009). This measure is typically applied to land use data, with the proportion of area that a land use type accounts for within a study unit being calculated. Besides, a few studies considered the proximity of urban functions, and found that the distances to specific functions as police stations, subway stations and parks could affect crime rate (Sohn, 2016b; Barnum et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022; Kim and Lee, 2023).
From previous literature, it was found that density, fraction and mix are the most frequently used measures of urban functions, correspond- ing to the three principal dimensions. Therefore, the present study fo- cuses on the three measures.
	Critical analysis of existing studies

While both land use data and POI data have been proven effective for crime prediction, there are several critical differences between the two data sources to be noted.
First, land use data often come from official sources, such as urban planning documents or remote sensing monitoring by the authorities, which featured with relatively high completeness and reliability but low update frequency. POI data, by contrast, are mainly produced from human activities and maintained by big-tech companies, and could be frequently update as urban functions change. However, as activity- oriented data, it might hardly provide enough information about pla- ces where people visit less, as well as private places such as dwellings. Second, the different geometric forms of land uses and POIs, i.e., polygons and points, would result in intrinsic difference in their spatial fidelity. Land use polygons can depict the sizes and shapes of urban function zones, and thus might work well for functions that spread across an area like residential ones. Nevertheless, facilities with small footprints are often omitted in land use data, and thus the data could hardly deal with multi-use areas. By contrast, POI data could present places within buildings and even rooms, and thus are fit for small-scale facilities like stores, ATMs and bus stations. However, the fidelity can be lost when representing larger function zones as points (Psyllidis et al., 2022). Some urban functions can be undertaken by spaces of divergent forms and scales, such as schools and recreation. Regarding their effects on crime, inconsistent findings have been drawn with land use data and POI data respectively, with no agreement on which data types should be used. Thorough studies are still needed to provide more directions on
which data to be used for each function type.
Third, regarding urban function classifications, those of land uses are generally coarser than those of POIs. It has been noted that land use data are far from ideal to differentiate establishments within a basic function category, especially commercial ones (Bowers, 2014). Empirical studies further show that different commercial facilities indeed have diverse effects on crime (O and Lee, 2016; Sohn, 2016a). Treating different land uses similarly could lead to conflicting findings because the combined category might mask potentially opposite effects (Stucky and Otten- smann, 2009). While POI data provide more detailed subcategories of several functions as commercial, business and recreation, it remains unknown whether the POI classifications are more suitable for studying their relationships with crime.
Last but not least, land use data and POI data provide different measures of urban functions due to their distinctive geometry forms. With land use data, previous studies usually evaluate urban function design and diversity with fractions and mix respectively. However, it is questionable to directly count land parcels without considering their sizes and shapes to indicate the strength of a function (Bowers, 2014), resulting in the missing of density feature. By contrast, POI data are

intrinsically suitable for evaluating function density since they represent facilities with countable points. POI fractions and POI mix can also be calculated in similar ways as land use ones, but they are less frequently
used in existing literature. It’s worth noting that the common measures
of land use and POI indeed correspond to different dimensions of the 3Ds, each of which has distinctive effects on crime, and improper measures might lead to misconceptions on the relationships between urban functions and crime. For example, both (Wang et al., 2016) and (Vomfell et al., 2018) have noted that POI fractions are generally less relevant in crime prediction compared with  POI densities. (Barnum   et al., 2017) tested both proximities and densities for each POI category as potential risk factors, and found that the optimal choice of feature vary across categories. Yet most previous researchers seem to choose urban function measures arbitrarily rather than carefully considering all the principal dimensions of the built environment.
In all, as POI data become increasingly popular in crime studies, there is an urgent need for systematic comparison on the effectiveness of POI data and land use data to avoid misleading results. Specifically, optimal data sources and measures should be determined with regard to urban function types.
	Data and methods

	Data and feature construction

	Study area, targeted crime type and analysis unit
This study was conducted for theft crime in Beijing, China. As the capital city of China, Beijing is a political, economic and cultural center with a vast area of 16,808 km2 and a large population of 20.46 million in
2020. The city is planned with a mono-centric spatial structure, with several ring roads surrounding the downtown area. Theft crime was chosen as representative of urban crime because it is one of the most
common  crime  types,  posing  great  threats  to  citizens’  possession.
Moreover, it could be easily affected by the built environment (He and Li, 2022). The study area was set within the 5th Ring Road of Beijing, where the majority of thefts occurred (Fig. 2). Both high density urban areas and low-density suburban areas are present within the range.
A raster grid with a resolution of 400 by 400 m was used as the analytic unit for this study, resulting in 4267 grid cells in total. While neighborhood-level crime studies often take street blocks as analytic unit, in the case of Beijing, street blocks in downtown and those in the outskirt have quite divergent sizes, and might confound the analysis of the spatial relationship between urban functions and crime. Besides, since many theft crimes are committed on the street, using streets as the boundaries of analytic units would lead to a dilemma as to which side those crimes should be assigned. Therefore, we chose the more homo- geneous grid cells with walkable size as the study unit, as adopted by previous researchers (Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009).
	Theft crime data
Complete legal documents of theft crimes, including written judge- ments, orders, notifications, etc., are available on the website China Judgements Online since the year 2014. Among these documents, a written judgement is the most comprehensive record for a case. In this study, we collected 10,246 written judgements of theft crimes in Beijing from 2014 to 2016. Most of the judgements record the detailed ad- dresses of the crime spots, while others hide them for privacy reasons. After filtering out those written judgements without address informa- tion, we extracted all available addresses from the documents using text identification codes, geocoded them with Gaode Location API and ob- tained the coordinate information of 6921 theft crimes. All the crime spots were mapped in ArcGIS, and 4182 of them fell within the study area.
We used spatial join to count the number of theft crime records within each 400 by 400 m grid in ArcGIS. The spatial distribution as well as the histogram of the theft crime counts is shown in Fig. 2. The theft

A R T I C L E I N F O  





	Introduction

As the urbanization process moves forward, the complexity and di- versity of urban contexts provide more chances for crime commitment (Zhu et al., 2022). As a result, urban crime becomes a global social problem that imposes serious economic burdens and social turbulence to city governments and citizens (He and Zheng, 2021; Batabyal and Beladi, 2022). Therefore, it is extremely important for city planners to implement proper planning policies to control crime and improve urban safety.
Urban function has long been recognized as an important environ- mental factor that related to local crime. Land use data, which represent land parcels as polygons and label them with urban function types, were commonly used for crime prediction and proven to be effective (Kinney et al., 2008; Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009). As big data reflecting city dynamics became widely available in recent years, point of interest (POI) data, which abstract physical facilities as points, have been pro- posed as a new data source for neighborhood function profiling and adopted by multiple urban crime studies (Zhao and Tang, 2017). Nevertheless, using either land use data or POI data, researchers came

up with conflicting findings about how urban functions affect crime. These inconsistencies would not only prevent researchers from utilizing data effectively in crime modelling, but also mislead urban planners as they endeavor to improve neighborhood security through appropriate organization of urban functions. To avoid such theoretical contradic- tions, it is of urgent need to systematically compare the performance of land use and POI indicators in crime prediction.
Several research gaps can be summarized. First, few researchers have discussed whether land use or POI data are more effective for crime

prediction at the neighborhood level.Second, there is little agreement on how to construct the most proper urban function indicators from land use or POI data. Third, it remains unknown whether POI indicators and land use indicators complement or conflict with each other in repre- senting different urban function. To fill these gaps, this paper conducts comparative experiments between land use and POI indicators, with regards to both urban function categories and measures, for theft crime prediction with a case study of Beijing, China. The results suggest the complementary use of land use and POI data, shedding light on how to construct more reliable urban function indicators for crime  prediction.
