	Literature review

	Relevant criminology theories

Various criminology theories have been developed to explain the occurrence of urban crime and provide prevention approaches, most of which consider place as a significant factor. For example, the routine activity theory suggests that the convergence of motivated offenders, suitable targets as well as the lack of capable guardian in specific space and time provides the conditions for crime commitment (Cohen and Felson, 1979). Furthermore, many theories emphasize the effect of environmental context. The broken windows theory points out that disorderly elements like broken windows, abandoned properties and litters indicate the lack of community control, and would eventually lead to more crime (Wilson and Kelling, 2017). The situation crime pre- vention (SCP) theory searches in the settings of crime occurrence for all kinds of proximate causes, such as access to facilities, natural surveil- lance, local laws and regulations, etc. (Shariati and Guerette, 2017). The theory of crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED) also asserts that crime incidents can be reduced by improving the quality of the built environment from several aspects such as access control, sur- veillance, target hardening, etc. (Cozens et al., 2005; Crowe and Zahm, 1994). In all, multiple theories have noted the effect of access to facil- ities, enlightening researchers to relate neighborhood function with local crime rate.
	Urban function data

As the completeness, granularity and availability of urban data gradually increased, thorough studies on the effects of urban functions on crime have become possible, in which land use data and POI data are two types of urban function data that are most commonly used.
Land use data, which represent land parcels as polygons and label them with urban function types, have long been used for modelling crime. Commonly, land use information can be derived from sources as satellite remote sensing and government authorities. While remote sensing images only reflect the natural properties of ground objects based on spectral characteristics (Yao et al., 2017), land use data from government authorities during planning activities emphasize the socio-economic functions of land parcels, and thus are more applicable for studying urban social phenomena such as crime. In this study, we focus on land use data of the latter category. The spatial units of urban land use data are generally street blocks or finer-grained parcels. As for time resolution, official land use data are often featured with relatively low update frequency, making it difficult for researchers to obtain up-to-date land use information that matches the time period of crime data, as in the cases of (Twinam, 2017) and (Wo, 2019).
POI data, which abstract physical facilities as points with socio- economic attributes, have emerged as an alternative to the conven- tional land use data for representing urban functions. Early crime studies obtained the geographic coordinates of commercial facilities from business data such as tax address data (Smith et al., 2000) and marketing website (Bernasco and Block, 2011), and it was not until the recent ten years that researchers started to collect massive POI data from map
service providers like Google’s Maps API (Bendler et al., 2014), Four-
Square (Wang et al., 2016; Zhao and Tang, 2017) and OpenStreetMap (Kadar et al., 2019) for better crime modelling. As a type of social sensing data, POI data are highly correlated with human activities. They record the locations, names and function types of places at the building level, and could be timely updated (Andrade et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022; Yue et al., 2017). Through machine learning, POI embeddings can further retain the latent semantic and spatial information of POIs and also make up for incomplete or inaccurate data (Yan et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2022). As the effectiveness of POI data in urban computing being recognized, they have gained increasing popularity in recent crime studies (Bendler et al., 2014; De Nadai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2016).

While POI data appear to have higher spatial and temporal resolution than land use data do, they do not necessarily lead to better explanations for the relationships between urban functions and crime. There are intrinsic differences between the two types of data in many aspects, such as their sources and forms, and they classify and represent urban func- tions in distinctive ways. Therefore, more thorough comparisons are needed before determining which type of data to use.
To attain a comprehensive knowledge of how previous researchers modelled crime with urban function indicators, related works are reviewed in terms of their focused functions, data, measures, main findings, etc. A summary of previous works by function categories is provided in Appendix A, Table A1.
	Urban function categories in relation to crime

Land use data and POI data resemble each other in the basic classi- fications of urban functions, among which residential and commercial functions are the most frequently studied ones. Other common function categories include business, education, transportation, recreation, pub- lic administration, etc. Nevertheless, POI data generally have much richer semantic features (Andrade et al., 2020), enabling further dif- ferentiation of urban functions. For example, FourSquare classifies POIs into ten parent categories and over 1000 subcategories (Foursquare, 2009). Using either land use data or POI data, researchers sometimes came up with divergent results when relating urban functions with crime. Main findings and controversies with regards to several common urban function categories are discussed as follows.
	Residential
Residential areas are perceived to be safer than non-residential ones, owing to informal social control from residents (Cozens et al., 2019). The majority of empirical studies also proved that residential land uses generally have negative relationships with various types of crime (Adel et al., 2016; Boessen and Hipp, 2018; Kinney et al., 2008; Sohn, 2016b; Su et al., 2023; Wo et al., 2024). Nevertheless, high-density residential areas are found to suffer from more crime (Kinney et al., 2008; Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009; Ando, Higuchi and Mimura, 2018). With POI
data, however, the effects of residence are sometimes overlooked. (Kim and  Lee, 2023)  didn’t found  notable relationships between residential
POIs and several crime types, and (Zeng et al., 2021) also found no effect of multi-story residences on theft crime, indicating that geographic points might be unsuitable for representing residential areas.
	Commercial
Whatever data were used, researchers generally concluded that commercial functions could significantly increase urban crime (Adel et al., 2016; Boessen and Hipp, 2018; Bowers, 2014; Kinney et al., 2008; Lockwood, 2007; Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009; Wilcox et al., 2004; Wo et al., 2024). However, the effects could vary across different commer- cial facilities (Sohn, 2016a). While land use data often treat all kinds of commercial uses as the same, POI data have more detailed classifications of commercial facilities, among which shops and restaurants are found to promote both property crime and violence (Bendler et al., 2014; De Nadai et al., 2020; Kim and Lee, 2023; O and Lee, 2016; Smith et al., 2000; Twinam, 2017; Vomfell et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021), alcohol-related places (bars, clubs and liquid stores) tend to attract vi- olent crimes rather than property ones (Bernasco and Block, 2011; He and Li, 2022; Smith et al., 2000; Vomfell et al., 2018), and hotels are less important (Zhang et al., 2022; Kim and Lee, 2023). In all, POI data could provide finer-grained pictures of the effects of various commercial fa- cilities on crime.
	Financial
Financial uses include business offices, banks and ATMs, etc. As for business function, office POIs are found to suppress theft crime and promote violent crime (Bendler et al., 2014; Kim and Lee, 2023; Smith

et al., 2000), yet previous studies failed to draw consistent conclusions with office land uses. While (Boessen and Hipp, 2018) suggested that office land uses result in higher level of several types of violence and property crime, (Wo et al., 2024) found positive effect of them on property crime and no effect on violence, and (Sohn, 2016a) suggested office land uses could decrease residential burglary. As for banks and ATMs, they are small-scale facilities and are generally represented with POI data, and most researchers found positive relationship of them with crime (Su et al., 2023; Yue et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2021).
	Education
The relationship between education functions and crime have been controversial. Theoretically, schools can either gather potential victims and attract motivated offenders, or produce positive socialization and guardians to improve neighborhood safety (Steinberg et al., 2019). In empirical studies, with POI data, most researchers believe that schools lead to more violent crime, while having no effect or negative effect on theft crime (Barnum et al., 2017; He et al., 2020; Vomfell et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022). With land use data, however, only some studies consider schools to be important factors triggering specific crime types like assault, property damage and motor vehicle theft (LaGRANGE, 1999; Wilcox et al., 2004; Kinney et al., 2008), while others found little effect of them on most crime types (Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009; Wo, 2019; He and Li, 2022).
	Transportation
For transportation function, most crime researchers focus on bus stops or subway stations using POI data, and claim them to be generators of various types of crime, especially property ones (Ando et al., 2018; Barnum et al., 2017; Bendler et al., 2014; He and Li, 2022; Kim and Lee, 2023; O and Lee, 2016; Yue et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). These transit stations are too small to be depicted with land use polygons. While transportation land uses can represent larger-scale transportation facilities like railway stations and airports, their effects on crime are seldom discussed.
	Recreation
Recreation functions can be undertaken by various forms of urban facilities including parks, playing fields, cultural facilities, etc. With land use data, recreation uses overall are found to increase crime rate (Wilcox et al., 2004; Lockwood, 2007; Kinney et al., 2008; Bowers, 2014), while parks seem to be insignificant (Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009; Sohn, 2016b; He and Li, 2022). By contrast, using POI data, parks, cultural and other entertainment facilities are all considered to be positively related with crime (Barnum et al., 2017; Bendler et al., 2014; He et al., 2020; Valente et al., 2024; Vomfell et al., 2018).
	Summary of inconsistencies
In summary, using either land use data or POI data, inconsistent findings have been drawn regarding the relationships of several urban functions with crime. For residential function, land use data seem to be more effective than POI ones. For education and office functions, more consistent findings can be derived from POI data rather than land use ones. For functions like commercial and recreation, the effects of the general categories are rather consistent using both data types, while POI data support further classifications and reveal that the subcategories indeed affect crime differently. Besides, some small-scale facilities like bus stations, banks and ATM can only be represented with POI data.
	Urban function measures in relation to crime

Beyond the classifications of urban functions, the measures of these functions also matter. To study routine activities and traffic patterns, (Cervero and Kockelman, 1997) have conceptualized the built envi- ronment into three principal dimensions, i.e., density, diversity and design (the 3Ds), with urban functions being an important part to be



Fig. 1. The 3Ds of urban function.

deconstructed. Fig. 1 illustrates the 3Ds with regard to urban functions. In criminology, the 3Ds are also thought to be able to change the mix of targets, offenders and guardians, and thus have great effect on criminal behaviors (Kim and Hipp, 2021).
Common measures of urban functions in empirical crime studies are consistent with the 3Ds as well, each of which has distinctive effect on crime. In this regard, density refers to how compact urban functions are. Compact neighborhoods are thought to either increase crime risk by
gathering more offenders and potential targets, or provide more natural surveillance through “eyes on the streets” (Jacobs, 1961; Kim and Hipp, 2021; Su et al., 2023). Since POI data present facilities as countable
points and could well support the measure of density, many studies calculate POI densities (or counts within an area) for various urban functions and relate them with crime. Most research find positive re- lationships between non-residential function density and crime rate, while the strength of effects vary across facility types (Bernasco and Block, 2011; O and Lee, 2016; De Nadai et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022).
Diversity refers to how mixed urban functions are. Similar to the case of density, there are debates on whether diversity has positive or negative impacts on crime. On the one hand, mixed functions bring about different times of use and ensure the presence of people, which could discourage potential offenders (Jacobs, 1961; Newman, 1972). On the other hand, the functional mix could be a cause of anonymity on the
streets, reducing people’s sense of responsibility and leading to higher
crime risk (Taylor et al., 1995). Several research have calculated land use mix with Herfindahl index or Shannon diversity index and examined their effect on crime, with divergent conclusions been drawn. Both (Jones and Pridemore, 2019) and (He and Li, 2022) believed that higher mix degree leads to more crime, while (Su et al., 2023) found the opposite. Other studies suggested that the impacts of land use mix vary across crime types as well as cities (Wo, 2019; De Nadai et al., 2020). Although the direct of effect remains controversial, previous studies generally agree that there are some relationships between functional mix and crime. As POI data gain popularity in recent years, researchers have just started to construct POI mix indicators for crime modelling (Kim and Lee, 2023), whose effectiveness needs to be further explored. Design refers to how urban functions are arranged, emphasizing the
provision as well as accessibility of amenities. By shaping pedestrians’
routines to their destinations, the design factors might bring offenders and targets together in specific space and time, facilitating crime commitment (Cohen and Felson, 1979; Cervero and Kockelman, 1997). Early studies constructed dummy variables to represent the existences of

specific urban functions, and found that the presence of facilities like malls, schools and playgrounds could lead to more crime (LaGRANGE, 1999; Wilcox et al., 2004). Later, fractions of urban functions became a more common measure to quantitatively depict the function composi- tions, enabling more accurate analysis on the effects of function pro- visions (Adel et al., 2016; Boessen and Hipp, 2018; Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009). This measure is typically applied to land use data, with the proportion of area that a land use type accounts for within a study unit being calculated. Besides, a few studies considered the proximity of urban functions, and found that the distances to specific functions as police stations, subway stations and parks could affect crime rate (Sohn, 2016b; Barnum et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022; Kim and Lee, 2023).
From previous literature, it was found that density, fraction and mix are the most frequently used measures of urban functions, correspond- ing to the three principal dimensions. Therefore, the present study fo- cuses on the three measures.
	Critical analysis of existing studies

While both land use data and POI data have been proven effective for crime prediction, there are several critical differences between the two data sources to be noted.
First, land use data often come from official sources, such as urban planning documents or remote sensing monitoring by the authorities, which featured with relatively high completeness and reliability but low update frequency. POI data, by contrast, are mainly produced from human activities and maintained by big-tech companies, and could be frequently update as urban functions change. However, as activity- oriented data, it might hardly provide enough information about pla- ces where people visit less, as well as private places such as dwellings. Second, the different geometric forms of land uses and POIs, i.e., polygons and points, would result in intrinsic difference in their spatial fidelity. Land use polygons can depict the sizes and shapes of urban function zones, and thus might work well for functions that spread across an area like residential ones. Nevertheless, facilities with small footprints are often omitted in land use data, and thus the data could hardly deal with multi-use areas. By contrast, POI data could present places within buildings and even rooms, and thus are fit for small-scale facilities like stores, ATMs and bus stations. However, the fidelity can be lost when representing larger function zones as points (Psyllidis et al., 2022). Some urban functions can be undertaken by spaces of divergent forms and scales, such as schools and recreation. Regarding their effects on crime, inconsistent findings have been drawn with land use data and POI data respectively, with no agreement on which data types should be used. Thorough studies are still needed to provide more directions on
which data to be used for each function type.
Third, regarding urban function classifications, those of land uses are generally coarser than those of POIs. It has been noted that land use data are far from ideal to differentiate establishments within a basic function category, especially commercial ones (Bowers, 2014). Empirical studies further show that different commercial facilities indeed have diverse effects on crime (O and Lee, 2016; Sohn, 2016a). Treating different land uses similarly could lead to conflicting findings because the combined category might mask potentially opposite effects (Stucky and Otten- smann, 2009). While POI data provide more detailed subcategories of several functions as commercial, business and recreation, it remains unknown whether the POI classifications are more suitable for studying their relationships with crime.
Last but not least, land use data and POI data provide different measures of urban functions due to their distinctive geometry forms. With land use data, previous studies usually evaluate urban function design and diversity with fractions and mix respectively. However, it is questionable to directly count land parcels without considering their sizes and shapes to indicate the strength of a function (Bowers, 2014), resulting in the missing of density feature. By contrast, POI data are

intrinsically suitable for evaluating function density since they represent facilities with countable points. POI fractions and POI mix can also be calculated in similar ways as land use ones, but they are less frequently
used in existing literature. It’s worth noting that the common measures
of land use and POI indeed correspond to different dimensions of the 3Ds, each of which has distinctive effects on crime, and improper measures might lead to misconceptions on the relationships between urban functions and crime. For example, both (Wang et al., 2016) and (Vomfell et al., 2018) have noted that POI fractions are generally less relevant in crime prediction compared with  POI densities. (Barnum   et al., 2017) tested both proximities and densities for each POI category as potential risk factors, and found that the optimal choice of feature vary across categories. Yet most previous researchers seem to choose urban function measures arbitrarily rather than carefully considering all the principal dimensions of the built environment.
In all, as POI data become increasingly popular in crime studies, there is an urgent need for systematic comparison on the effectiveness of POI data and land use data to avoid misleading results. Specifically, optimal data sources and measures should be determined with regard to urban function types.
	Data and methods

	Data and feature construction

	Study area, targeted crime type and analysis unit
This study was conducted for theft crime in Beijing, China. As the capital city of China, Beijing is a political, economic and cultural center with a vast area of 16,808 km2 and a large population of 20.46 million in
2020. The city is planned with a mono-centric spatial structure, with several ring roads surrounding the downtown area. Theft crime was chosen as representative of urban crime because it is one of the most
common  crime  types,  posing  great  threats  to  citizens’  possession.
Moreover, it could be easily affected by the built environment (He and Li, 2022). The study area was set within the 5th Ring Road of Beijing, where the majority of thefts occurred (Fig. 2). Both high density urban areas and low-density suburban areas are present within the range.
A raster grid with a resolution of 400 by 400 m was used as the analytic unit for this study, resulting in 4267 grid cells in total. While neighborhood-level crime studies often take street blocks as analytic unit, in the case of Beijing, street blocks in downtown and those in the outskirt have quite divergent sizes, and might confound the analysis of the spatial relationship between urban functions and crime. Besides, since many theft crimes are committed on the street, using streets as the boundaries of analytic units would lead to a dilemma as to which side those crimes should be assigned. Therefore, we chose the more homo- geneous grid cells with walkable size as the study unit, as adopted by previous researchers (Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009).
	Theft crime data
Complete legal documents of theft crimes, including written judge- ments, orders, notifications, etc., are available on the website China Judgements Online since the year 2014. Among these documents, a written judgement is the most comprehensive record for a case. In this study, we collected 10,246 written judgements of theft crimes in Beijing from 2014 to 2016. Most of the judgements record the detailed ad- dresses of the crime spots, while others hide them for privacy reasons. After filtering out those written judgements without address informa- tion, we extracted all available addresses from the documents using text identification codes, geocoded them with Gaode Location API and ob- tained the coordinate information of 6921 theft crimes. All the crime spots were mapped in ArcGIS, and 4182 of them fell within the study area.
We used spatial join to count the number of theft crime records within each 400 by 400 m grid in ArcGIS. The spatial distribution as well as the histogram of the theft crime counts is shown in Fig. 2. The theft

POI data were crawled from the Gaode Map API (Amap, 2016) in the year 2016. As one of the most popular map service providers in China, Gaode Map provides rather complete POI data within the nation, which have been widely used in urban studies (Psyllidis et al., 2022; Wang   et al., 2022). The Gaode POI data record the geographical coordinates, names and categories of real-world places, for navigation as well as other location-based services. As point proxies of places, the Gaode POIs are generally the geometric centroids of urban function areas (Wu et al., 2022).

	Geographically weighted negative binomial regression (GWNBR)
One possible limitation of the above regression models is their poor consideration of spatial non-stationarity, which means that the re- lationships between the predictors and the target variable may vary over space. To deal with the spatial non-stationarity of crimes, geographically weighted regressions are possible alternatives to the global regression methods (Cahill and Mulligan, 2007). As localized regression models, they estimate the model parameters specifically for each spatial unit, with closer regions having greater influence than the farther ones do.
They are also effective in reducing the model’s bias from the spatial
autocorrelation effect. In this work, the Geographically Weighted Negative Binomial Regression Model (GWNBR) is used to determine whether the effects of neighborhood functions on urban crimes exhibit spatial heterogeneity based on different indicators. The formula for the GWNBR model is:
	yi = NB[eXiβi ,   ki]	(9)
where yi and Xi represents the theft crime count and the crime predictors for the ith grid cell, while βi and ki are the negative binomial regression coefficients and the shape parameter estimated for the grid cell.
In consideration of the spatial structure, the GWNBR model applies weights to the neighborhood grid cells within a specific bandwidth. Cross validation (CV) and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) are commonly used to search for the optimal bandwidth. While CV carries out an iterative process to find the bandwidth that maximizes the model accuracy, AIC approach pursues compromise between the accuracy and

	Each urban function variable was added to the baseline regres- sion model separately, and the AIC value after adding the variable was recorded;
	All the urban function variables were ranked by the model AIC values (lowest to highest) from step (a);

Only when a variable was significant (p<0.1) and reduced the model AIC by over 1, and it was neither strongly correlated with the former reserved predictors (Pearson correlation coefficient < 0.6) nor making any of them insignificant, it would enter the final model.
In consideration of spatial heterogeneity, we further applied GWNBR models to evaluate the spatial variation of predictive powers for different urban function indicators. Since the main purpose was to compare different measurements for the same urban function, we only focused on the LU_FRAC, POI_DEN and POI_FRAC variables specific for each function type in the GWNBR analysis. The basic urban features were combined with the LU_FRAC, POI_DEN and POI_FRAC variables respectively to construct comparative models. The local significances and coefficients for each urban function variable could indicate where it was most effective for theft crime prediction and how it was related to theft crime locally.

To get an intuitive impression on both land use and POI data, we first visualized the spatial distributions of land use parcels and POIs for four typical urban functions, including residential, commercial, education, and green space. As shown in Fig. 5, the two types of data have both similarities and divergences in representing urban functions. The dis- tributions of residential lands and residence POIs are highly coincident with each other, except that residence POIs are relatively sparser in both downtown area and the outskirts. By contrast, the distribution of shop and catering POIs is much denser than that of commercial lands. These POIs are not confined to the planned commercial areas, but often spread over streets and mix with other urban functions. The same is true for the education function. Though both land use and POI data show that ed- ucation facilities gather in the northwest of the study area, education POIs have a broader scope ranging from schools, tutoring centers to training agencies, etc., and they are distributed more extensively in the city. For green spaces, on the contrary, land use data provides more detailed knowledge on their shapes and sizes, while POI data marks only particular sites where visitors frequently check in and thus seems incomplete.
For more detailed comparison, we also selected some typical grids to visualize their land use and POI distributions, as well as their land use fractions, POI fractions and POI densities. As shown in Fig. 6, these features depict urban functions in quite different ways and could lead to divergent results. First, land use data can provide a relatively complete function profile for an area, while POI data highlight facilities along streets, especially commercial ones, and contain much less information of private places like dwellings, as exemplified by grid (A), (C), (D) and (E). Second, land use data are sometimes too simplified to represent the actual condition of mixed-use land as POI data can do. For example, grid

Similarly, grid (F) is located in a university and thus categorized as education land, but there are indeed various kinds of POIs such as dormitories, shops and health facilities. 	NBR model results

The performances of NBR models are shown in Table 1. The baseline model, i.e., NBR Model 0, obtained an AIC of 10,233.4 and a BIC of 10,277.9. The NBR Model 1 and 2 decreased the AIC value from the baseline model by 439.8 and 141.5 respectively, indicating that both POI indicators and land use indicators could improve the accuracy of
theft crime prediction, while the former ones were more effective. The performances of NBR Model 3–7 further revealed that density, fraction
and diversity features from both POI and land use  were  useful  theft crime predictors, but with distinctive predictive power. The AIC and BIC values gave the same ranking for their predictive power, which was POI_DEN > POI_FRAC > POI_MIX > LU_FRAC > LU_MIX. POI indicators
from any one of the measures obtained better performance than the land use indicators did. Density features, which can only be constructed from the POI data, were the most effective among all the measures, with NBR Model 3 decreasing the AIC by 409.3 from the baseline. The diversity features generally had weaker predictive power than the density and fraction features.
NBR Model 8 combined some of the most effective predictors from both POI and land use data through the feature selection procedure, and obtained the lowest BIC among all the models. Although NBR Model 1 obtained a slightly lower AIC value than NBR Model 8 did, it was heavily penalized under the BIC criterion for its additional parameters. Thus, NBR Model 8 is a more correct model.

police station, education, hotel, nightlife and bank with theft crime, while POI_DEN has obvious advantage in the government agency func- tion. For shop and catering POIs and public facility POIs, the local co- efficients of POI_DEN indicators are featured with fewer significant grids but larger magnitude. Thus, the density features for these functions should be attached great importance in specific places.

While POI data and land use data have both been used to represent urban functions in crime prediction, a direct comparison between their predictive powers has been virtually nonexistent. To fill the gap, this study focused on the comparison between POI data and land use data with regard to three measures of urban functional features, i.e., density,

In total, 5 categories of urban functional indicators (i.e., land use fractions, land use mix, POI den- sities, POI fractions, and POI mix) were constructed and applied in comparative experiments with a case study in Beijing. The results indi- cate that different data source and feature construction methods could

lead to divergent knowledge on the relationships between urban func- tions and theft crime. Therefore, a guidance is of urgent need to explain whether POI data or land use data to use, and how to use them in theft crime prediction.

	Data source

As shown by our case study, land use data is generally less effective than POI data in theft crime modelling, whatever models are used. As the crowdsourced POI data become popular recently, many studies have noticed that the involvement of POI data can largely improve crime modelling performance, especially for theft crime (Bendler et al., 2014; Vomfell et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016), but none have discussed whether POI data outperform the conventional land use data.

map service providers to keep up with the change of urban functions. For another thing, land use data, as segmented polygons, cannot effectively capture mixed function types. For example, a residential land parcel might include both dwelling units and ancillary facilities, such as con- venience  stores, restaurants and gyms,  etc.  While such information is

usually omitted in land use data, POI data, in the form of points, are much more flexible to show mixed and multiple uses even at the building level (Yue et al., 2017).

	Measures of urban functions
The 3Ds’ theory suggests that density, diversity and design are different characteristics of the built environment (Cervero and Kockel- man, 1997), each of which has distinctive effects on crime (Kim and
Hipp, 2021). While density, mix and fraction are all common measures of urban functions, previous researchers seldom noticed the fact that these measures indeed correspond to different dimensions of the 3Ds.

Grids with similarThe present study suggests that density is the most effective measure for theft crime prediction, followed by fraction and mix respectively. Existing research also found that POI densities generally outperform POI fractions when relating specific urban functions with crime (Vomfell  et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016). Although a large fraction value could reflect the predominance of a specific urban function, it fails to depict the absolute intensity of that function as density does.
land use fractions or POI fractions might indeed have distinctive mag-

nitudes of facilities.For example, a grid in the outskirts with m shops and n medical stores has exactly the same POI fractions as a grid in the downtown area with 2m shops and 2n medical stores does, but the latter one is obviously more prosperous than the former one. The fact that density features can only be extracted from POI data further explains its

superior predictive power over land use data. By reserving information about the compactness of urban functions, POI densities can more accurately reflect the magnitude of human activities, which has more direct impacts on theft crime occurrence.
Diversity features are shown to be positively related with theft crime by our experiment. The results are consistent with the majority of existing literature (Jones and Pridemore, 2019; He and Li, 2022; Kim and Lee, 2023), though some argue that the impact of diversity could vary across cities and crime types (Wo, 2019; De Nadai et al., 2020). While most previous studies evaluate function diversity using land use data, our study further reveals that POI mix outperforms land use mix in crime prediction. Nevertheless, both land use mix and POI mix are synthetic indexes independent of urban function types, and thus have limited predictive power compared with density and fraction features.
	Tailoring features for different function types

Although POI density features generally have the strongest predic- tive power, they cannot capture the effects of all the urban functions on theft crime. Actually, the optimal data and measure are not unified but specific for each urban function.
First, some land use types are too aggregated, while POI data provide more detailed subcategories to differentiate their effects on crime. Pre- vious studies have proposed that the broad function categories might mask potentially opposite effects of specific facilities (Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009), and highlighted the needs to make further classi- fications for urban functions like commercial ones (Sohn, 2016a). Beyond the existing literature, we further discovered that the sub- categories of commercial (shop and catering, hotel and nightlife), financial (enterprise and bank) and administration (government agency and police station) all have distinctive impacts on theft crime, with regression coefficients of different magnitudes and even signs. For these functions, POI data outperform land use ones for crime modelling with their abundant subcategories.
Second, the scales of facilities matter in determining whether land use polygons or POIs are fit for representing specific urban functions. As revealed by our results, land use data have advantage in capturing the relationships of culture, green space and transportation functions with theft crime. These land uses are typically comprised of housing estates, museums, parks, railway stations, airports, etc., which usually occupy large areas in the urban layout and thus can be better represented by polygons rather than points. By contrast, POI data are fit for small-scale facilities like bus stations, banks, enterprises and shops. The mismatch of facility scales and representation forms might lead to inaccurate findings on their relationships with crime. For example, while previous studies generally found that office POIs can suppress theft crime and promote violent crime (Bendler et al., 2014; Kim and Lee, 2023; Smith et al., 2000), controversial results were drawn with office land uses (Boessen and Hipp, 2018; Sohn, 2016a; Wo et al., 2024). The reason might be that a majority of enterprises are microscale ones, and their offices usually dotted over urban spaces rather than being confined to business zones, and thus office land uses are not sufficient to capture the function. Another common mismatch is to represent residential zones with POIs. Since the abstract points erase information of shapes and sizes, they cannot define the boundaries of the residential zones, nor can it differ- entiate between large housing estates and small ones. While the effects of residential land uses on crime have long been recognized, with POI data, researchers sometimes failed to detect significant relationships (Kim and Lee, 2023; Zeng et al., 2021).
Third, while existing studies generally measured POIs by density, our
research suggests that the fraction matters more for some urban func- tions in crime modelling, as in the cases of education, shop and catering, police stations, enterprises and banks. These are mostly common daily facilities and their numbers often rise acutely in highly populated areas. Therefore, their absolute densities could hardly reflect whether these functions are truly dominating in a specific area as POI fractions do. For

example, a prosperous residential community might be equipped with many educational facilities like kindergartens, primary schools and tutoring centers, yet education is only an auxiliary function for the community. By contrast, education-dominated neighborhoods such as university towns could have similar POI density but much higher POI fraction for education spots, as exemplified by grid(C) and grid(F) in Fig. 6. It is the latter type of neighborhoods that provide abundant sites for youths to gather and hold activities, and are much easier to become the target of thieves (Kinney et al., 2008; Willits et al., 2013).
Finally, the POI densities of medical, nightlife, hotels, government agencies, public facilities and bus stations are useful for theft crime prediction, most of which has been proven effective in previous studies (Ando et al., 2018; Bendler et al., 2014; De Nadai et al., 2020; O and Lee, 2016; Vomfell et al., 2018; Yue et al., 2024). These facilities are generally less sensitive to local population, e.g., a dense community does not necessarily have many nightlife spots. Moreover, medical, nightlife and hotels are crime attractors featured with cash economies and weakly guarded targets, providing very specific opportunities for property crime (Bernasco and Block, 2011), and thus their numbers have direct impact on theft crime rate.
	Spatial heterogeneity

While numerous studies have been conducted to explore the effects of urban functions on crime, they generally adopted non-spatial models, assuming that the urban function variables operate identically over space. However, it has been proposed that the non-stationarity of spatial processes cannot be overlooked in crime modelling (Cahill and Mulli- gan, 2007).
By applying the GWNBR models, this study reveals that the re- lationships of urban function variables with crime vary significantly with location, and further highlights the necessity to consider spatial non-stationarity when choosing between land use indicators and POI ones for theft crime modelling. None of the indicators can model the relationships between urban functions and theft crime throughout the study area, and different indicators for even the same urban function could have diverse spatial patterns of effect. For one thing, urban functions themselves affect crime differently as the spatial context change. For example, traffic stations are homogeneously distributed in most of the study area, but they are much sparser in the southern area, which makes them more prominent for thieves as target places of crime. Thus, both the POI_FRAC and POI_DEN for traffic stations have the strongest positive effects on theft crime in the southern area. However, these POI indicators are not as important as the LU_FRAC for trans- portation in the eastern area, where lots of transportation hubs exist. For another thing, facilities categorized as the same urban function might be in quite different forms across urban area. For example, culture POIs are densely distributed in the east side of the study area, most of which are private small-scale galleries such as those in the 798 Art District. How- ever, these places are seldom defined as culture land in the land use planning. The 798 Art District, transformed from the former state-owned electronic factories, is still categorized as industrial land in the planning data. In the west side of the study area, by contrast, many large-scale culture and recreation sites exists in the forms of libraries, stadiums, theatres, etc., most of which are documented in the land use planning. As a result, the POI_FRAC for culture is effective theft crime predictor in the eastern area, while the LU_FRAC for culture has significant impacts in the western area. Besides, it can also be noted that LU_FRAC variables are  seldom  effective for  theft crime prediction in the  downtown area,
while  POI  indicators  have  better  performance.  The  most  possible
explanation is that the downtown area is featured with small blocks and dense traditional buildings carrying highly mixed urban functions, and land use data could hardly reflect these functions as completely as POI data do.
In general, the choice between POI and land use for theft crime modelling might be specific for different urban context, especially for

urban functions like culture, medication, park and transportation, and for urban areas with different density and diversity. Nevertheless, POI and land use indicators could also be complementary in revealing the effects of urban functions in heterogeneous urban area through careful discussion and tailoring from region to region.
	Implications

This research focuses on the notable problem that the use of POI data and land use data could lead to divergent results when modelling the relationships between urban functions and theft crime. To address this, several useful insights are provided for urban crime prediction and planning policy making.
First, as indicated by the NBR and GWNBR models’ performance, POI
densities are effective predictors in theft crime prediction. While the organization of urban functions has been proven to be closely related to crime occurrences, it might be difficult to acquire up-to-date and high- resolution land use data for many cities. Fortunately, POI  data are  now highly accessible through map service platforms, providing timely and detailed profiles of urban functions and becoming a potential sub- stitute to land use data. Under proper feature construction methods, they can obtain even stronger predictive power.
Second, the superiority of POI density features over fraction and diversity ones indicates that the intensity of urban functions has notable impacts on theft crime rate. While previous urban plannings are generally coarse organizations of different land use types, this study suggests that the density of facilities in a function zone should be also taken into consideration. For example, among commercial lands, those where nightlife spots gather tend to trigger more theft crimes, so limiting the density and business hours of nightlife spots might be of great help to reduce theft crime rate.
Third, for different urban functions or even the same urban function with different forms of facilities, the optimal choice between POI in- dicators and land use indicators could be divergent. This could be attributed to several factors, such as the scale and properties of facilities, the spatial context, etc. Therefore, to obtain comprehensive knowledge about the associations of urban functions with theft crime as well as to make more accurate prediction, POI data and land use data should be used for different functions and in different places as complement to each other. In the practice of urban function planning, it is also neces- sary to combine land use planning with facility planning when dealing with different function types. For example, while arranging land parcels for large-scale transportation and cultural infrastructures like railway stations and museums, the POI distributions for smaller-scale facilities like bus stations and private galleries should also be taken into consideration.
Last but not least, our findings regarding the power of POI data and land use data in urban modeling might be applied in topics other than crime study. With a case study of theft crime prediction, we fully dis- cussed how to choose between POI data and land use data and how to further construct proper features to depict different urban functions. These rules might be also useful for modeling other phenomenon asso- ciated with urban functional organizations, like urban vitality and attraction.
	Limitations and future directions

This study also has some limitations that need to be addressed in future research.
First, land use data and POI data used in this study were generated in different years (2014 and 2016 respectively). Although we used theft crime data from 2014 to 2016 accordingly and the time gap is not large, the inconsistency of data collection time might still have some effects on the comparison results.
Second, we only considered three most commonly used measures, i. e., density, fraction and diversity, when constructing POI and land use

indicators. However, other types of urban function features like prox- imity were also used in previous crime studies and proved to be effective (Barnum et al., 2017). Moreover, representation learning have also merged as a novel and promising approach to produce both POI and land use features (Yan et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2022). For future studies, more up-to-date feature construction methods should be taken into account to make a more thorough comparison between land use data and POI data.
Third, the predictive powers of urban function indicators may vary at different spatial granularity. For example, (Sypion-Dutkowska and Leitner, 2017) pointed out that the strong influence of land use types on crime is limited to a distance of 50 m. Since this study is specific for the 400-by-400-meter gridded urban areas, further researches should be conducted to make clear how to choose urban functional indicators as the spatial granularity of crime prediction changes.
Fourth, the accuracy of POI data has a direct impact on its effec- tiveness. Although the POI data we used is maintained by the big-tech company Gaode Map and is widely recognized in Chinese urban studies, the unavailability of Chinese official cadastral data make it hard to quantitatively evaluate the data accuracy. For future studies, the effectiveness of POI data should be discussed with regards to its error margin.
Fifth, while demographic features are generally considered as important factors affecting crime rate, the lack of fine-grained popula- tion data in our case makes it hard to capture the effects accurately. For future studies, mobile phone signaling data, as a finer-grained substi- tution to the traditional census data, can be applied for better control of demographic factors. Furthermore, the data might help to propose some benchmarks as to what urban functions are less sensitive to local pop- ulation and thus can be better depicted by POI densities rather than POI fractions.
Last, this study is conducted specifically for theft crime. More re- searches are needed to reveal if the findings in this study remain true for other types of urban crime.
	Conclusion

As proposed by the urban mosaic model, cities can be seen as a mosaic of land uses and activities, and the arrangement of urban functions
would largely shape  people’s routines  and destinations,  having  great
impact on socio-economic activities (Kinney et al., 2008). Urban func- tion data have long been applied in modelling various socio-economic phenomena, among which urban crime is one of the most frequently studied topics. Early studies mainly relied on land use data from official sources, and it was not until the recent decade that the crowdsourced POI data gained popularity in modelling crime. However, there are intrinsic differences between the two types of data in many aspects as their geometric forms, fidelity, measures, etc. Using different data and measures have led to divergent findings on the relationships of urban functions with crime. Therefore, a guidance is of urgent need regarding which data to use, and how to use them. To fill the gap, this study sys- tematically compares the effectiveness of land use and POI data for theft crime modelling with regard to three commonly used measures, i.e., density, fraction and diversity. Several findings can be summarized.
First, among the two types of urban function data, i.e., land use and POI, the latter one could provide generally more effective predictors for crime prediction. While both data have being widely used for modelling
crime,  there  hasn’t been a  direct comparison of  their effectiveness in
existing literature. As a type of social sensing data, POIs record the lo- cations of built-up facilities at the building level and can be frequently updated, and thus have much higher spatial and temporal fidelity compared with the conventional land uses drafted in the plans for urban development, contributing to their advantage in crime modelling.
Second, the three measures of urban functions, i.e., density, fraction and mix, have different predictive power on crime occurrences, with density being the strongest in general. Notably, density features can only

be constructed from POI data. Although these measures are all commonly used for crime modelling, previous studies seldom noticed that they correspond to different dimensions of the built environment, i. e., density, design and diversity (the 3Ds), each having distinctive effects on crime. This explains why previous researchers obtained different outcomes with POI densities and POI fractions respectively (Vomfell et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016). Careful consideration of all the principal dimensions is advocated when constructing urban function features.
Third, the optimal data source and measure is specific for each urban function. For commercial, financial and administrative functions, POI data surpass land use ones by providing more detailed subcategories to differentiate their effects on crime. The too aggregated land use types might mask potentially opposite effects of different facilities (Stucky and Ottensmann, 2009). The scales of facilities are also critical for deciding whether land use or POI data to use. Land use data, in the form of polygons with shapes and sizes, provide better depictions for residential, culture, green space and transportation functions that spread across an area. By contrast, POI data are abstract points and are fit for small-scale facilities like bus stations, banks, enterprises and shops. The mismatch of facility scales and representation forms could lead to inconsistent find- ings on their relationships with crime, as in the cases of residence and office. Furthermore, while most researchers intuitively measured POIs by density for crime modelling, the present study found that the fraction matters more for some urban functions as education, shop and catering, police stations, enterprises and banks. These are common daily facilities, and their densities fluctuate with local population rather than reflecting the strength of the functions themselves, while POI fractions can depict whether the functions are truly dominating an area. By contrast, POI densities perform better for facilities that are more specific or less sen- sitive to local population, such as government agencies, medication, nightlife and stations.
Last but not least, POI and land use data can be used complemen-
tarily to each other for theft crime modelling in heterogeneous urban context. While existing studies generally adopted non-spatial models, assuming the relationships between various urban functions and crime to be identical over space, our research suggest the necessity to consider spatial heterogeneity. The effects of urban functions on crime vary significantly with location, and the optimal choice of function indicators also depends on the local context, especially for those functions under- taken by distinctive forms of space like culture, medication, park and transportation, and for places with different density and diversity. Specifically, POI data perform better in denser, more mixed-used regions

with smaller-scale facilities, while the opposite is true for land use data. Beyond the traditional approaches of representing urban functions with singular data type and measure, we construct and compare urban function features from both land use and POI data across three critical measures, i.e., density, fraction, and diversity. Through the dual lenses of NBR and GWNBR, this study not only finds POI densities generally more effective compared to the other indicators, but also unveils that the optimal choice of data sources and feature measures is intimately tied to the specific urban functions and spatial narratives. Moreover, this study highlights the complementary use of land use and POI data in crafting urban functions with regards to the heterogeneity of urban space, which was seldom considered in existing research. Through this lens, the studies provide a refined blueprint for urban planners and researchers to craft precise urban function indicators, which would not only contribute to predicting urban crime and making prevention strategies, but also serve as a methodological guide for exploring various urban-function-
related phenomena.

1.  Introduction     Each Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) message is either a request    or a response.  A server listens on a connection for a request,    parses each message received, interprets the message semantics in    relation to the identified request target, and responds to that    request with one or more response messages.  A client constructs    request messages to communicate specific intentions, examines    received responses to see if the intentions were carried out, and    determines how to interpret the results.  This document defines    HTTP/1.1 request and response semantics in terms of the architecture    defined in [RFC7230].     HTTP provides a uniform interface for interacting with a resource    (Section 2), regardless of its type, nature, or implementation, via    the manipulation and transfer of representations (Section 3).     HTTP semantics include the intentions defined by each request method    (Section 4), extensions to those semantics that might be described in    request header fields (Section 5), the meaning of status codes to    indicate a machine-readable response (Section 6), and the meaning of    other control data and resource metadata that might be given in    response header fields (Section 7).     This document also defines representation metadata that describe how    a payload is intended to be interpreted by a recipient, the request    header fields that might influence content selection, and the various    selection algorithms that are collectively referred to as "content    negotiation" (Section 3.4).  1.1.  Conformance and Error Handling     The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",    "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this    document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC2119].     Conformance criteria and considerations regarding error handling are    defined in Section 2.5 of [RFC7230].  1.2. Resources     The target of an HTTP request is called a "resource".  HTTP does not    limit the nature of a resource; it merely defines an interface that    might be used to interact with resources. Content-Location     The "Content-Location" header field references a URI that can be used    as an identifier for a specific resource corresponding to the    representation in this message's payload. Fielding & Reschke           Standards Track                   [Page 15]RFC 7231             HTTP/1.1 Semantics and Content            June 2014      If Content-Location is included in a 2xx (Successful) response    message and its value refers (after conversion to absolute form) to a    URI that is the same as the effective request URI, then the recipient    MAY consider the payload to be a current representation of that    resource at the time indicated by the message origination date. If the user agent had    wanted the latter semantics, it would have applied the PUT directly    to the Content-Location URI.  3.2.  Representation Data     The representation data associated with an HTTP message is either    provided as the payload body of the message or referred to by the    message semantics and the effective request URI.  The representation    data is in a format and encoding defined by the representation    metadata header fields.     The data type of the representation data is determined via the header    fields Content-Type and Content-Encoding.  These define a two-layer,    ordered encoding model:       representation-data := Content-Encoding( Content-Type( bits ) )  3.3.  Payload Semantics     Some HTTP messages transfer a complete or partial representation as    the message "payload".  In some cases, a payload might contain only    the associated representation's header fields (e.g., responses to    HEAD) or only some part(s) of the representation data (e.g., the 206    (Partial Content) status code).     The purpose of a payload in a request is defined by the method    semantics.  For example, a representation in the payload of a PUT    request (Section 4.3.4) represents the desired state of the target    resource if the request is successfully applied, whereas a    representation in the payload of a POST request (Section 4.3.3)    represents information to be processed by the target resource.       Fielding & Reschke           Standards Track                   [Page 17]RFC 7231             HTTP/1.1 Semantics and Content            June 2014      In a response, the payload's purpose is defined by both the request    method and the response status code.  For example, the payload of a    200 (OK) response to GET (Section 4.3.1) represents the current state    of the target resource, as observed at the time of the message    origination date (Section 7.1.1.2), whereas the payload of the same    status code in a response to POST might represent either the    processing result or the new state of the target resource after    applying the processing.  Response messages with an error status code    usually contain a payload that represents the error condition, such    that it describes the error state and what next steps are suggested    for resolving it.     Header fields that specifically describe the payload, rather than the    associated representation, are referred to as "payload header    fields".  Payload header fields are defined in other parts of this    specification, due to their impact on message parsing.     +-------------------+----------------------------+    | Header Field Name | Defined in...              |    +-------------------+----------------------------+    | Content-Length    | Section 3.3.2 of [RFC7230] |    | Content-Range     | Section 4.2 of [RFC7233]   |    | Trailer           | Section 4.4 of [RFC7230]   |    | Transfer-Encoding | Section 3.3.1 of [RFC7230] |    +-------------------+----------------------------+  3.4.  Content Negotiation     When responses convey payload information, whether indicating a    success or an error, the origin server often has different ways of    representing that information; for example, in different formats,    languages, or encodings.  Likewise, different users or user agents    might have differing capabilities, characteristics, or preferences    that could influence which representation, among those available,    would be best to deliver.  For this reason, HTTP provides mechanisms    for content negotiation.     This specification defines two patterns of content negotiation that    can be made visible within the protocol: "proactive", where the    server selects the representation based upon the user agent's stated    preferences, and "reactive" negotiation, where the server provides a    list of representations for the user agent to choose from.  Other    patterns of content negotiation include "conditional content", where    the representation consists of multiple parts that are selectively    rendered based on user agent parameters, "active content", where the    representation contains a script that makes additional (more    specific) requests based on the user agent characteristics, and    "Transparent Content Negotiation" ([RFC2295]), where content    Fielding & Reschke           Standards Track                   [Page 18]RFC 7231             HTTP/1.1 Semantics and Content            June 2014      selection is performed by an intermediary.  These patterns are not    mutually exclusive, and each has trade-offs in applicability and    practicality.     Note that, in all cases, HTTP is not aware of the resource semantics.    The consistency with which an origin server responds to requests,    over time and over the varying dimensions of content negotiation, and    thus the "sameness" of a resource's observed representations over    time, is determined entirely by whatever entity or algorithm selects    or generates those responses.  HTTP pays no attention to the man    behind the curtain.  3.4.1.  Proactive Negotiation     When content negotiation preferences are sent by the user agent in a    request to encourage an algorithm located at the server to select the    preferred representation, it is called proactive negotiation (a.k.a.,    server-driven negotiation).  Selection is based on the available    representations for a response (the dimensions over which it might    vary, such as language, content-coding, etc.) compared to various    information supplied in the request, including both the explicit    negotiation fields of Section 5.3 and implicit characteristics, such    as the client's network address or parts of the User-Agent field.     Proactive negotiation is advantageous when the algorithm for    selecting from among the available representations is difficult to    describe to a user agent, or when the server desires to send its    "best guess" to the user agent along with the first response (hoping    to avoid the round trip delay of a subsequent request if the "best    guess" is good enough for the user).  In order to improve the    server's guess, a user agent MAY send request header fields that    describe its preferences.     Proactive negotiation has serious disadvantages:     o  It is impossible for the server to accurately determine what might       be "best" for any given user, since that would require complete       knowledge of both the capabilities of the user agent and the       intended use for the response (e.g., does the user want to view it       on screen or print it on paper?);     o  Having the user agent describe its capabilities in every request       can be both very inefficient (given that only a small percentage       of responses have multiple representations) and a potential risk       to the user's privacy;     o  It complicates the implementation of an origin server and the       algorithms for generating responses to a request; and,    Fielding & Reschke           Standards Track                   [Page 19]RFC 7231             HTTP/1.1 Semantics and Content            June 2014      o  It limits the reusability of responses for shared caching.     A user agent cannot rely on proactive negotiation preferences being    consistently honored, since the origin server might not implement    proactive negotiation for the requested resource or might decide that    sending a response that doesn't conform to the user agent's    preferences is better than sending a 406 (Not Acceptable) response.     A Vary header field (Section 7.1.4) is often sent in a response    subject to proactive negotiation to indicate what parts of the    request information were used in the selection algorithm.  3.4.2.  Reactive Negotiation     With reactive negotiation (a.k.a., agent-driven negotiation),    selection of the best response representation (regardless of the    status code) is performed by the user agent after receiving an    initial response from the origin server that contains a list of    resources for alternative representations.  If the user agent is not    satisfied by the initial response representation, it can perform a    GET request on one or more of the alternative resources, selected    based on metadata included in the list, to obtain a different form of    representation for that response.  Selection of alternatives might be    performed automatically by the user agent or manually by the user    selecting from a generated (possibly hypertext) menu.     Note that the above refers to representations of the response, in    general, not representations of the resource.  The alternative    representations are only considered representations of the target    resource if the response in which those alternatives are provided has    the semantics of being a representation of the target resource (e.g.,    a 200 (OK) response to a GET request) or has the semantics of    providing links to alternative representations for the target    resource (e.g., a 300 (Multiple Choices) response to a GET request).     A server might choose not to send an initial representation, other    than the list of alternatives, and thereby indicate that reactive    negotiation by the user agent is preferred.  For example, the    alternatives listed in responses with the 300 (Multiple Choices) and    406 (Not Acceptable) status codes include information about the    available representations so that the user or user agent can react by    making a selection.     Reactive negotiation is advantageous when the response would vary    over commonly used dimensions (such as type, language, or encoding),    when the origin server is unable to determine a user agent's    capabilities from examining the request, and generally when public    caches are used to distribute server load and reduce network usage.    Fielding & Reschke           Standards Track                   [Page 20]RFC 7231             HTTP/1.1 Semantics and Content            June 2014      Reactive negotiation suffers from the disadvantages of transmitting a    list of alternatives to the user agent, which degrades user-perceived    latency if transmitted in the header section, and needing a second    request to obtain an alternate representation.  Furthermore, this    specification does not define a mechanism for supporting automatic    selection, though it does not prevent such a mechanism from being    developed as an extension.  4.  Request Methods4.1.  Overview     The request method token is the primary source of request semantics;    it indicates the purpose for which the client has made this request    and what is expected by the client as a successful result.     The request method's semantics might be further specialized by the    semantics of some header fields when present in a request (Section 5)    if those additional semantics do not conflict with the method.  For    example, a client can send conditional request header fields    (Section 5.2) to make the requested action conditional on the current    state of the target resource ([RFC7232]).       method = token     HTTP was originally designed to be usable as an interface to    distributed object systems.  The request method was envisioned as    applying semantics to a target resource in much the same way as    invoking a defined method on an identified object would apply    semantics.  The method token is case-sensitive because it might be    used as a gateway to object-based systems with case-sensitive method    names.     Unlike distributed objects, the standardized request methods in HTTP    are not resource-specific, since uniform interfaces provide for    better visibility and reuse in network-based systems [REST].  Once    defined, a standardized method ought to have the same semantics when    applied to any resource, though each resource determines for itself    whether those semantics are implemented or allowed.
